Rapidus in Japan targets 2 nm in 2027. The concentration is not an accident: a leading-edge node costs ~$20–30 billion of fab plus several billion in R&D, and the amortization worked example above shows why only the firm with the most customers can afford it: an empty fab pays ~$10,000 of depreciation per wafer, a full one ~$5,000.

Money is only the first of three reasons the position is so hard to attack; the other two are physical. The second is **yield learning**. A new node does not start at D0 = 0.1/cm²: it starts several times higher, and D0 falls only as wafers are run, failing dies are cut open, each defect mechanism is traced to a tool or recipe and removed, one mechanism at a time (Module 13). That learning needs volume, volume needs customers, and customers only commit to a node whose yield is already known, so the firm with the most wafers learns fastest and pulls further ahead each generation; TSMC's ~1.4 million wafer starts a month are a learning rate as much as a revenue line. The third is that a node is not a blueprint but ~1,000 tuned recipes and the several thousand engineers who tuned them. Moving it to a new site means copying every recipe and re-qualifying every tool ("Copy Exactly", in Intel's phrase; Module 05) with a workforce that has not yet seen the failure modes, which is why Arizona trails Tainan by years on the same node, and why the design side is tied to the same place: designers only design for a node with a proven **PDK** (process design kit, the rulebook describing what the fab can make; step 2 of the master flow) and a mature library of tested circuit blocks, and those exist first, and sometimes only, for the node with the most customers.

> **What can go wrong: a node that does not ramp, and an island that shakes.** The best-documented failure is a node that misses its yield schedule: Intel's 10 nm process, planned for 2015–2016, did not reach healthy yields until 2019, and its foundry ambitions and product roadmap paid for the gap for years, and Samsung's 3 nm-class node, the first to use gate-all-around nanosheets, was widely reported to have struggled with yield in its first years, which is a large part of why it struggled for external customers (Module 05). The geographic failure mode is seismic. Taiwan's fabs sit on base isolation and every tool shuts down on a seismic trigger, scrapping only the wafers mid-process; after the magnitude 7.4 Hualien earthquake of April 2024 TSMC reported most tools recovered within a day and full production within ~3 days, at a cost well under 1% of a quarter's revenue (Module 20). That is the manageable case. The tail case, a larger quake near Tainan or a blockade, has no recovery time to quote, which is why customers and governments fund fabs in Arizona, Japan and Germany that cost more per wafer than Taiwan's.

Module 05 and Module 20 explain how a **GIGAFAB** (TSMC's name for a site of 100k+ wpm) is organized and what the concentration risk means.

### 3. Advanced packaging and HBM: the AI-era bottleneck

For AI accelerators specifically, the tightest constraint from 2023 through 2026 has been neither EUV nor wafers but the two steps *after* the wafer: CoWoS capacity and HBM supply. Both are hard for the same reason: they are new, high-value process flows with **yield learning curves**, and the demand for them roughly quadrupled in two years. A new flow starts with failure modes nobody has seen, and yield improves only by running material and fixing what fails, one mode at a time; so capacity that exists on paper, as installed tools, is not the same as capacity that yields, and the gap closes over quarters, not weeks. TSMC's CoWoS ramp from ~35k to ~120–140k wafers per month (end-2024 to end-2026 target, as of mid-2026) required entire new fabs (AP7 in Chiayi, AP8 in Tainan), and even so analysts estimated a supply gap of ~20% entering 2026, narrowing toward ~10% as the new sites ramp.

On the memory side, published HBM bit-share and revenue-share estimates are not directly interchangeable, and SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron each diverted a large slice of DRAM wafer capacity to HBM. An HBM die needs more wafer area per stored bit than an ordinary DRAM die: each die gives up area to TSV columns and the keep-out zones around them, carries a much wider interface and more redundancy, and the stack needs a base die that stores nothing at all. As a rule of thumb an HBM bit consumes roughly 3x the wafer area of a DDR5 bit (Module 15 puts the die-area part alone at ~1.5–1.8x, with the base die, stacking losses and spares making up the rest), so a hypothetical 5% of bits at three times the wafer area per bit would consume about 14% of a two-product wafer mix, and more at SK hynix, which is why ordinary DRAM prices rose sharply in 2025–2026. HBM4, with its 2,048-bit interface and logic base die made at TSMC or Samsung foundry rather than in the DRAM fab, ships in volume for Rubin in 2026. Modules 15 and 17 cover the mechanisms.

> **What can go wrong: capacity on paper versus capacity that yields.** A CoWoS line or an HBM stacking line is specified in wafers per month of tool capacity, but its output is that number times a yield that starts low. A new interposer size, a new bonding film, or a twelve-high stack instead of eight-high each reset part of the learning curve, and the difference between 60% and 90% stacking yield is a third of the world's HBM. Analysts' capacity numbers are tool counts; the shipment numbers that matter lag them by the time it takes to learn.

There is a fourth candidate chokepoint that is cheaper but no less absolute, and it is a side note here and Module 20's subject: Japanese materials. Japan supplies ~90% of **photoresist** (the light-sensitive coating that lithography patterns), ~55–60% of silicon wafers, most **mask blanks** (the flat, ultra-pure quartz plates, carrying a reflective multilayer for EUV, on which each mask's stencil is written; Hoya and AGC), and 100% of ABF (Ajinomoto).

None of these is expensive, and none is protected by a monopoly on the underlying chemistry. What protects them is **qualification lock-in**. A resist or a blank is not a commodity bought by specification; it is tuned into each layer's recipe over months of test wafers, and its exact formulation, batch behaviour and defect statistics are baked into that layer's **process window** (the range of dose, focus and etch settings over which the layer still prints and yields; a new material shifts the window, and every setting tuned to the old one has to be found again). Changing supplier means re-qualifying every affected layer, which for a resist used on dozens of layers is a multi-year program with yield risk at every step, so no fab does it unless forced. Modules 04 and 20 return to it.

## Master Process Flow: Sand to Rack in ~60 Steps

This is the spine of the course. Each step is at the granularity of "STI formation" or "M1 dual damascene," the level at which fab engineers talk about the flow; later modules expand each into its unit processes (litho, etch, deposition, clean, metrology). Where a step repeats many times it appears once with a note. Each step has a first line naming it the way engineers do and a second line in plain language saying what physically happens and why, with every acronym expanded at first use. You are not expected to retain the sub-items on first read; the step names and their order are the point.

**Vocabulary for this list**, recapped from the primer:

- The six unit processes: deposit a film, pattern it by lithography, etch it, implant dopants, polish flat (CMP), clean and measure. Every fab step below is a loop of these.
- Transistor parts: source, drain, channel, gate; the gate is insulated from the channel by a thin dielectric (an insulator).
- A **via** is a vertical hole filled with metal joining two wiring levels; a **trench** is the groove that becomes a wire.
- A **hard mask** is a tougher stencil layer (a nitride or carbon film) into which the resist pattern is first transferred, because resist alone is too soft and thin to survive a deep etch.
- An **anneal** is a heat treatment that repairs crystal damage and activates dopants (settles them into lattice sites where they conduct).

**Stage 0: Design and masks (Module 19, Module 04)**

1. Architecture and RTL design; verification (Synopsys, Cadence tools; ~2–4 years for a new GPU)  
   Architects decide what the chip does; designers write it as **RTL** (register-transfer level code, a text description of every storage element and the logic between them); verification engineers simulate it for years, because a bug found after the masks are written costs tens of millions of dollars and months.
2. Synthesis, place and route, timing closure, DRC/LVS signoff against the foundry PDK  
   Software turns the RTL into transistors and wires (synthesis), decides where each of billions of them sits (place) and how they connect (route), adjusts until every signal arrives on time (timing closure), and checks the drawing against the foundry's rulebook, the **PDK** (process design kit: the files describing what the fab can make), with **DRC** (design rule check: are all shapes wide enough and far enough apart?) and **LVS** (layout versus schematic: do the drawn shapes form the intended circuit?).
3. Tape-out: GDSII/OASIS layout; OPC and mask data prep (compute-intensive, weeks)  
   **Tape-out** is the moment the finished layout (a **GDSII** or **OASIS** file, the two standard formats describing every polygon on every layer) goes to the foundry. **OPC** (optical proximity correction) then pre-distorts every polygon so that, after the blurring of the lens, what prints is what was drawn.
4. Mask making: e-beam write (multi-beam, ~10–20 h per critical layer), etch, inspect, repair, pellicle; a full N3/N2 mask set costs ~$20–30M+  
   Each layer's corrected pattern is written into an absorber film on a quartz plate by an electron beam (**multi-beam**: a writer such as IMS Nanofabrication's splits the beam into ~262,144 beamlets that write in parallel, because a single beam flashing the pattern one rectangle at a time would take days per mask), etched, inspected pixel by pixel, repaired where a defect is found, and covered with a **pellicle** (a transparent membrane that keeps dust out of the focal plane). Why a set costs tens of millions: the mask is drawn at 4× the wafer scale, but after OPC its pattern is far denser than the drawn layout, with correction features smaller than anything that prints, and every feature over the ~100 cm² of the plate must be right, since a single defect prints on every field of every wafer; an EUV mask blank (Hoya, AGC) carries the same Mo/Si multilayer as the scanner mirrors, and a buried bump a few nanometers high in that stack prints as a defect, so blanks are inspected with 13.5 nm light itself (Lasertec) and blanks with no printable defect are rare and priced accordingly; and an EUV pellicle must be a membrane tens of nanometers thick that passes ~90% of the light while surviving the source's heat. Masks are made in the foundries' own mask shops and by Photronics, Tekscend (formerly Toppan) and DNP; the writers come from IMS Nanofabrication (Austria, Intel-owned) and NuFlare (Japan). Module 04 covers the flow.

**Stage 1: Raw material to wafer (Modules 01–03)**

5. Quartz mining and beneficiation  
   Quartz rock is blasted, crushed, washed and sorted (**beneficiation**: raising the ore's grade by physical separation) into lumps of >98% SiO2; the deposit's trace boron and phosphorus decide what the lumps are good for.
6. Carbothermic reduction to MG-Si (submerged arc furnace)  
   Quartz and carbon are heated by an electric arc at ~2,000 °C; the carbon takes the oxygen away as CO, and liquid silicon of 98–99% purity is tapped from the furnace bottom.
7. Hydrochlorination of MG-Si to trichlorosilane  
   Ground MG-Si reacts with HCl gas at ~300 °C in a fluidized bed to make TCS, a liquid; the silicon is now in a form that can be distilled.
8. Multi-column distillation of TCS to 9N–11N  
   The TCS is boiled and recondensed through a series of tall columns; each pass leaves behind impurities with higher or lower boiling points, until the wrong atoms are down to parts per trillion.
9. Siemens CVD deposition of polysilicon rods (or FBR granules)  
   Pure TCS and hydrogen flow over silicon rods heated to ~1,100 °C in a bell jar; the gas decomposes and silicon deposits on the rods for 3–5 days (or, in an FBR, onto floating seed granules that grow into beads).
10. Rod harvest, crushing, etch-clean, packaging  
    The rods are broken into chunks, etched to strip surface contamination picked up in handling, and sealed in bags; from here on, every touch is a contamination risk.
11. Crucible charge and melt-down (Czochralski puller, Ar, ~1,420 °C)  
    ~400 kg of chunks are loaded into a quartz crucible, the chamber is filled with argon so nothing oxidizes, and the heater melts the charge over several hours.
12. Seed dip, Dash neck, shoulder, body growth (MCZ), tail, cooldown  
    A seed crystal touches the melt, a thin neck is pulled to shed dislocations, the crystal is widened to 300 mm (the shoulder), the 2 m body is pulled at ~0.5–1 mm/min under a magnetic field that steadies the melt, the diameter is tapered off (the tail) to avoid thermal shock, and the ingot cools for hours.
13. Ingot crop, diameter grind, notch, resistivity/orientation test  
    The seed and tail ends are cut off, the body is ground to exactly 300 mm, a notch is ground along its length to mark the crystal orientation for every later machine, and resistivity (which reveals the dopant concentration) and orientation are measured.
14. Diamond-wire multi-wire sawing into wafers  
    A single ~100 km diamond-coated wire wound into a web of parallel strands is drawn through the ingot, cutting ~1,500–2,000 slices at once over many hours.
15. Lapping/grinding, edge rounding, damage etch  
    The saw leaves the slices wavy and cracked in their top microns; lapping between abrasive plates makes them flat and parallel, the sharp edge is rounded so it will not chip, and a chemical etch dissolves the cracked layer.
16. Double-side polish and front-side finish CMP  
    Both faces are polished to remove the last roughness, then the front face gets a final chemical-mechanical polish to an atomically smooth surface, the one the fab will print on.
17. RCA clean, laser mark, flatness/particle inspection; epitaxial layer growth if specified  
    The two-step RCA chemistry strips particles and metals, a laser scribes an identification code, the wafer is measured for flatness and scanned for particles, and if ordered a few µm of ultra-pure silicon are grown on top by CVD to bury crystal defects.
18. Ship in cassettes/FOUPs to fab  
    Wafers are sealed in cassettes or FOUPs under nitrogen, and the wafer maker's job ends. Value so far: ~$100–150.

**Stage 2: FEOL, transistor formation (Modules 05–11; each step includes its own litho/etch/clean/metrology loop)**

19. Incoming clean; zero-layer alignment mark etch  
    The wafer is cleaned on arrival and the first pattern ever printed on it is a set of alignment marks, etched into the silicon, to which every one of the ~100 later layers will be positioned.
20. Channel material prep: for GAA nanosheets, epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattice (3–4 pairs); for FinFET, none  
    For a **gate-all-around (GAA)** transistor, alternating layers of silicon and silicon-germanium (**SiGe**), each a few nm thick, are grown on the surface; the SiGe layers are sacrificial and will later be removed to leave the silicon sheets that become channels. A FinFET carves its channel from the bulk wafer.
21. Fin/nanosheet-stack patterning: hard-mask deposition, EUV or SAQP mandrel/spacer patterning, high-aspect-ratio Si etch  
    A hard mask is deposited, the fin pattern is printed by EUV or by **SAQP** (self-aligned quadruple patterning: print one line, the **mandrel**, coat its sides with a spacer film, remove the mandrel, repeat, so one printed line becomes four at a quarter of the pitch), and a deep **high-aspect-ratio** etch (aspect ratio is height divided by width; the fins are many times taller than they are wide, which is hard because the etching gas must reach the bottom of a narrow slot and the etched by-products must get back out) cuts tall thin fins or stacks into the silicon. (See the worked example on EUV tool count in the wafer fab section.)
22. **STI formation**: liner oxidation, flowable/HARP oxide fill, STI CMP, oxide recess (fin reveal)  
    **STI** (shallow trench isolation) fills the gaps between fins with oxide so neighbouring transistors cannot leak into each other: a thin oxide liner is grown, the gaps are filled with an oxide that flows in as a liquid-like film (**flowable** CVD oxide) or with **HARP** (high-aspect-ratio process, Applied Materials' name for a CVD oxide that fills narrow deep gaps without leaving voids), the excess is polished off, and the oxide is etched back to expose the top of each fin.
23. Well and Vt implants (n-well, p-well, anti-punch-through), anneal  
    Ions of boron or phosphorus are fired into selected regions to create the **wells** (the p-type or n-type background each kind of transistor sits in), to set each device's **threshold voltage (Vt)** (the gate voltage at which it switches on), and to add a buried doped layer that stops current sneaking beneath the channel (**anti-punch-through**); an anneal then repairs the damage and activates the dopants.
24. Dummy gate stack: dummy oxide, amorphous-Si deposition, hard mask, gate patterning (EUV), gate etch  
    A temporary **dummy gate** of **amorphous silicon** (silicon deposited with no crystal order, its atoms jumbled like a glass, which deposits smoothly and etches cleanly) is built where the real gate will go, because the real gate materials would not survive the high-temperature steps that follow (the **gate-last** flow); it is printed with EUV and etched. (See the worked example on EUV tool count.)
25. Gate spacer: ALD low-k SiOCN, anisotropic spacer etch  
    A thin insulating film of silicon oxycarbonitride (**SiOCN**, chosen for its low dielectric constant) is deposited by **ALD** (atomic layer deposition: one atomic layer per gas pulse, perfectly conformal) over everything, then etched straight down (an **anisotropic** etch) so it remains only on the gate's vertical sidewalls, as the **spacers** that set the distance from gate to source/drain.
26. Source/drain recess etch; inner-spacer formation for GAA (SiGe lateral recess, ALD fill, etch-back)  
    The silicon either side of the gate is etched away to make room for the source and drain; in a GAA device the SiGe layers are also recessed sideways under the spacers and the pockets refilled with insulator (**inner spacers**), which will insulate the future gate from the source and drain.
27. Embedded epitaxial S/D: SiGe:B for PMOS, Si:P for NMOS (selective epi, ~600–700 °C)  
    The source and drain are regrown as crystal, boron-doped SiGe for p-type (**PMOS**) transistors and phosphorus-doped silicon for n-type (**NMOS**), deposited only on exposed silicon (selective epitaxy); the SiGe also squeezes the channel (strain), which makes holes move faster.
28. Contact etch-stop liner (SiN) and ILD0 (flowable oxide) deposition; CMP to expose dummy gate top  
    A silicon nitride liner is laid down as the layer later contact etches will stop on, the surface is buried in the first **inter-layer dielectric (ILD0)**, an oxide insulator, and CMP planarizes it until the tops of the dummy gates show.
29. **Replacement metal gate** (gate-last): dummy (poly)silicon removal; for GAA, channel release (selective SiGe etch); interfacial SiO2; ALD HfO2 high-k; work-function metals (TiN, TiAlC, TiN); W or Co fill; gate CMP  
    The dummy gate is dissolved out, leaving a trench (it is the amorphous-silicon film of step 24, which has crystallized into polysilicon during the anneals since, so engineers call it "dummy poly"); in a GAA device the SiGe between the silicon sheets is etched away too, so each sheet hangs free (**channel release**); a few atomic layers of SiO2 are grown, then **hafnium oxide (HfO2)**, a **high-k** dielectric (high dielectric constant: it insulates like a very thin oxide while being physically thicker, which stops gate leakage), is deposited by ALD around every sheet; **work-function metals** (titanium nitride and titanium aluminum carbide, whose choice sets the threshold voltage) are deposited; the trench is filled with tungsten or cobalt and polished flat. The transistor is now complete.
30. Gate cut; gate recess and self-aligned contact cap (SiN)  
    The long gate lines running across many fins are cut into individual gates, and each gate's metal is recessed and capped with nitride so that a later contact etch landing slightly off-target hits insulator rather than gate metal (a **self-aligned contact**).

**Stage 3: MOL, contacts (Modules 11–12)**

31. Trench-silicide/contact patterning (EUV), etch to S/D epi  
    The holes and slots for the contacts are printed by EUV and etched down through ILD0 to the source/drain crystal.
32. Contact metallization: Ti/TiN liner, TiSix formation, Co/W/Ru fill, CMP  
    Titanium and titanium nitride are deposited into the holes and heated so the titanium reacts with the silicon into **titanium silicide (TiSix)**, a low-resistance junction between metal and semiconductor; the holes are filled with cobalt, tungsten or ruthenium and polished.
33. Gate contact and V0 via: patterning, etch, fill, CMP  
    A second set of holes connects to the gates, and **V0**, the zeroth via level, brings every contact up to the height of the first wiring level.

**Stage 4: BEOL, interconnect (Module 12; steps 34–35 repeat ~15–18 times with loosening pitch)**

34. **M0/M1 formation**: low-k dielectric deposition, EUV single-expose or SALELE patterning, trench etch, TaN barrier/Ru or Co liner or Cu seed, Cu electroplate (or direct Ru/Mo for M0), CMP, dielectric cap  
    The first wiring levels are the finest in the chip: low-k insulator is deposited, the line pattern is printed by a single EUV exposure or by **SALELE** (self-aligned litho-etch-litho-etch: two interleaved EUV exposures in which a spacer defined by the first aligns the second), trenches are etched, a TaN barrier and a ruthenium or cobalt liner are deposited, a copper seed is sputtered and the trench is electroplated full of copper (or, at M0, filled directly with ruthenium or molybdenum, which need no barrier), the excess is polished off, and a thin dielectric cap seals the copper. (See the worked example on EUV tool count.)
35. **Mx dual damascene** (via + trench in one fill), ~24–28 nm pitch at M1–M2, DUV immersion multi-patterning at intermediate levels, single-expose DUV at global levels  
    Each subsequent level is built by dual damascene: the via holes and the trenches above them are etched first, then both are filled with copper in one plating step and polished. M1–M2 are printed with EUV; intermediate levels use DUV immersion with two or more exposures per layer; the wide top levels use a single DUV exposure. This block repeats ~15–18 times.
36. Top thick metals and RDL (Al or thick Cu), MIM capacitors if used  
    The top levels are thick aluminum or copper lines carrying power across the die, plus a **redistribution layer (RDL)** that fans the connections out to the bump positions and, where used, **metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors**, thin sandwiches of metal and dielectric that smooth the on-chip power supply.
37. Passivation (SiN/SiO2 stack), polyimide, bond-pad opening  
    The finished wiring is sealed under nitride and oxide (**passivation**) and a soft polyimide layer against moisture and scratches, and windows are etched open over the pads where the bumps will go.
38. (A16/PowerVia-class nodes) backside power delivery: bond to carrier wafer, flip, thin to ~<1 µm over devices, nano-TSV etch and fill, backside power rail metallization  
    On the newest nodes the power wires move to the *back* of the wafer: it is bonded face-down to a carrier, flipped, thinned until less than a micrometer of silicon remains under the transistors, tiny **nano-TSVs** are etched through to the transistors' contacts, and power rails are built on the backside, freeing the front-side wiring for signals. Intel's version is **PowerVia**.

**Stage 5: Wafer test and preparation (Modules 13–14, 16)**

39. Inline metrology and inspection at every critical layer (CD-SEM, OCD, overlay, bright-field/e-beam defect inspection); parametric test on scribe-line structures  
    After each critical layer, sample wafers are measured: a **CD-SEM** (critical-dimension scanning electron microscope) measures line widths; **OCD** (optical critical dimension, or scatterometry) infers feature shapes from how light scatters; overlay tools measure how well the layer landed on the one below; optical and electron-beam inspectors scan for particles and pattern errors. Test transistors in the **scribe lines** (the strips between dies that will be cut away) are probed to check the electrical parameters of the process itself.
40. **Wafer sort**: probe-card contact, ATE test, wafer map, redundancy repair/e-fuse, binning  
    Every die is contacted and tested, spare blocks are switched in for dead ones by blowing **e-fuses** (tiny on-chip fuses that permanently record a configuration), and each die is assigned a bin. (See the worked example on die per wafer and yield in the Wafer sort section.)
41. Bumping: UBM sputter, resist pattern, Cu pillar/microbump plating (~40 µm pitch for CoW; C4 ~130–150 µm for direct-on-substrate)  
    An **under-bump metallization (UBM)** stack is sputtered over the pads, a resist pattern opens holes over each pad, and copper pillars or solder microbumps are electroplated up through the holes.
42. Backgrind (with tape/protective film), stress-relief etch, backside metal if required  
    The front is protected with tape, the back is ground from 775 µm to the target thickness, a light etch removes the grinding damage (which would otherwise weaken and warp the die), and a metal film is added on the back if the package needs it for heat or electrical contact.
43. Dicing (laser groove + blade, stealth laser, or plasma), die pick and place into trays  
    The wafer is cut along the scribe lines, and each good die, identified from the wafer map, is picked up by a vacuum nozzle and placed in a tray.

**Stage 6: HBM (Module 15; runs in parallel in the memory maker's fab)**

44. DRAM wafer fab (~1T1C cell, 1β/1γ node, EUV on 1–5 layers) with via-middle TSV formation  
    The DRAM wafers are made in a memory fab: each bit is a **1T1C** cell (one transistor and one capacitor, the capacitor holding the charge that stores the bit), on the makers' **1β** or **1γ** generations (the current DRAM node names), with EUV on a few of the finest layers. The TSVs are formed **via-middle**, etched and filled after the transistors but before the wiring, so the wiring can be built over them.
45. Base (logic) die fab, on DRAM process for HBM3/3E or on foundry logic node (TSMC N12/N5, Samsung) for HBM4  
    The base die at the bottom of each stack is made separately: on the DRAM process for HBM3 and HBM3E, and for HBM4 on a real logic node at a foundry, so it can carry the faster and more complex interface.
46. TSV reveal: wafer thinning to ~30 µm on carrier, backside bump  
    Each DRAM wafer is glued to a carrier, ground to ~30 µm so the buried TSV columns poke out of the back, and given bumps on that back face too, so it can be stacked on and under.
47. Die-to-wafer stacking: 8/12/16-high by TC-NCF, MR-MUF, or hybrid bonding  
    Thinned DRAM dies are placed one on another on a base-die wafer, 8, 12 or 16 high, and bonded by one of the three methods described in the HBM section.
48. Stack test and burn-in; **known-good stacked die** (KGSD) shipment  
    Each stack is tested and burned in as a unit and ships only if it passes (the KGSD guarantee), because a bad stack found later scraps a whole GPU package.

**Stage 7: Advanced packaging (Module 17)**

49. Substrate fabrication (parallel): core drilling and plating, sequential ABF build-up (~10–20 layers, laser vias, SAP plating), solder mask, surface finish  
    In a separate factory, a glass-fibre core is drilled and plated, then ABF layers are laminated one at a time, each laser-drilled for vias and patterned by **SAP** (semi-additive process: a thin seed metal, a resist pattern, plating only where wanted, then seed removal), to build ~10–20 layers of copper wiring; a solder mask and a surface finish protect the pads.
50. Interposer fabrication: Si interposer with TSVs and 3–4 Cu layers (CoWoS-S), or RDL interposer with embedded LSI bridges (CoWoS-L)  
    The interposer is made in the fab with the same tools as a chip but with no transistors: for CoWoS-S, a silicon wafer with TSVs and three or four copper wiring layers; for CoWoS-L, a molded wafer with fine RDL wiring and **LSI bridges** (local silicon interconnect: small silicon dies carrying only wiring, embedded where the GPU and HBM meet).
51. **Chip-on-wafer**: flip-chip TC bonding of GPU die(s) and HBM stacks onto interposer wafer; underfill; molding; overmold grind  
    The GPU dies and HBM stacks are placed face-down on the interposer wafer and bonded by **thermo-compression (TC) bonding** (heat and pressure applied to each die so its bumps fuse to the interposer pads), the gaps are underfilled, the wafer is encased in mold compound (**overmold**) and the top is ground flat. (See the worked example on CoWoS wafers to packages.)
52. Interposer wafer thinning and TSV reveal; C4 bumping; CoW dicing  
    The interposer wafer is thinned from the back until its TSVs are exposed, given the larger C4 bumps that will connect to the substrate, and cut into individual modules. (See the worked example on CoWoS wafers to packages: this is where ~16 or ~29 packages per wafer is decided.)
53. **Wafer-on-substrate**: CoW module reflow onto ABF substrate; underfill  
    Each module is placed on its substrate and passed through a reflow oven that melts the C4 bumps; the gap is underfilled.
54. Lid or stiffener attach with thermal interface material; BGA ball attach; laser mark  
    A copper lid (or a **stiffening ring**, a metal frame glued around the edge of the substrate to hold it flat when the package has no lid and will be cooled through the bare die) is glued on over a **thermal interface material (TIM)**, the paste or soft metal that carries heat from die to lid; a grid of solder balls (**BGA**, ball grid array) is attached to the bottom; the part is laser-marked. This is the packaged GPU.

**Stage 8: Final test and system (Modules 18–19)**

55. Package final test (ATE); burn-in; speed/power binning  
    The package is tested in a socket by ATE, burned in, and sorted by the clock speed it reaches and the power it draws.
56. System-level test in socket with real workloads  
    The GPU runs actual software, with real memory and drivers, for hours, to catch failures that pattern tests miss.
57. SXM module assembly: GPU package onto module PCB with VRMs; reflow; test  
    The package and its voltage regulators are soldered to the SXM board in a reflow oven and the module is tested.
58. Board integration: HGX baseboard (8 GPU + NVSwitch) or GB200/GB300 compute tray (2 Grace + 4 Blackwell), cold plates  
    Modules are mounted on a baseboard or tray with the NVSwitch chips, CPUs, and the cold plates that will carry the water cooling.
59. Rack integration: 18 compute trays + 9 NVSwitch trays, NVLink copper spine, busbar, CDU/manifolds; rack burn-in and cluster test  
    Trays slide into the rack, ~5,000 copper NVLink cables connect them through the spine, a **busbar** (a thick copper bar running the height of the rack) distributes DC power to every tray, the CDU and its **manifolds** (the pipes that split the coolant to each tray) are connected, and the whole rack runs for days under load before shipping.
60. Data center deployment: power, liquid cooling, InfiniBand/Ethernet fabric and optics, bring-up, cluster validation  
    Racks are installed, connected to power, water, and the network fabric of switches and optical links, and the cluster is brought up and validated as a single machine.

If you memorize one thing from this module, memorize this list.

## How to Read This Course

The course is organized in the order the material flows. Each module is self-contained enough to read alone, but the flow list above is the index: find the step you care about, and its module is listed beside it. For any term you meet and cannot place, Module 21 is the glossary.

**Part I: Raw materials and wafers**

- **Module 01, Sand to Polysilicon.** Steps 5–10. Quartz mining, the submerged arc furnace, trichlorosilane chemistry and distillation, the Siemens reactor in detail, FBR, purity measurement at 11N, and who makes what.
- **Module 02, Crystal Growth.** Steps 11–13. Czochralski from crucible to cooldown, why the Dash neck works, oxygen and carbon control, MCZ, dopant segregation, the point-defect physics (vacancies, interstitials, COPs, the V/G criterion), Float Zone, and why 450 mm died.
- **Module 03, From Ingot to Polished Wafer.** Steps 14–18. Wire sawing, lapping, edge rounding, double-side polish, CMP, RCA cleaning, flatness metrics (SFQR, GBIR), epitaxy, SOI by Smart Cut, and the five-company wafer oligopoly.
- **Module 04, Beyond Silicon and Fab Consumables.** SiGe, SiC, GaN, GaAs, InP; then everything the fab consumes: photoresists, specialty gases, wet chemicals, ultrapure water, CMP slurries, sputter targets, quartzware, and the photomask flow (blanks, writers, OPC, pellicles). Supports Step 4 and every step in Stages 2–4.

**Part II: The front end**

- **Module 05, Inside a Leading-Edge Fab.** The building, cleanroom, AMHS, tool layout, wafer starts, cycle time, cost structure, and how TSMC organizes a GIGAFAB. Frames Steps 19–39.
- **Module 06, Thermal Oxidation and Thin-Film Deposition.** Deal-Grove, furnaces, RTP, CVD variants, ALD half-reactions, PVD, epitaxy. Used in nearly every step from 20 to 37.
- **Module 07, Photolithography I: Resist and DUV.** Resist chemistry, the track, Rayleigh's equation, immersion at NA 1.35, OPC, phase-shift masks, LELE/SADP/SAQP multi-patterning, overlay. Used at every patterning step.
- **Module 08, Photolithography II: EUV in Full Detail.** The 13.5 nm source, tin droplets, Mo/Si mirrors, reflective reticles, stochastics, EUV resists, pellicles, throughput, High-NA, ASML's supply chain, and export controls. Steps 21, 24, 31, 34, 35.
- **Module 09, Etch.** Plasma physics, RIE, CCP vs ICP, anisotropy and selectivity, passivation, high-aspect-ratio etch, atomic layer etch, endpoint detection. Steps 21–22, 24–26, 29, 31–35.
- **Module 10, Doping.** Ion implantation from source to anneal, channeling, damage, RTA/laser anneal, diffusion, in-situ doped epi. Steps 23, 27.
- **Module 11, Building a Transistor.** MOSFET operation, short-channel effects, HKMG, gate-last, strain, FinFET, GAA nanosheets, backside power, CFET, and what "2 nm" actually means. Steps 20–33 and 38, walked as one flow.
- **Module 12, Interconnect (BEOL).** Copper dual damascene step by step, barriers and liners, low-k, Ru/Co/Mo, RC delay, electromigration, backside power delivery, and MOL contacts. Steps 31–38.
- **Module 13, Metrology, Inspection, and Yield.** Ellipsometry, CD-SEM, OCD, overlay, defect inspection, SPC, yield models, D0, die-size vs yield, learning curves. Step 39, and the reason every other step is measurable.
- **Module 14, Wafer Sort and Test.** Probe cards, ATE, test economics, binning, e-fuses, known-good die, DFT. Step 40.

**Part III: Memory**

- **Module 15, DRAM, NAND, and HBM Manufacturing.** The 1T1C cell and its capacitor, 1α/1β/1γ nodes, EUV in DRAM, 3D NAND channel-hole etch and string stacking, and HBM from TSV to 16-high hybrid-bonded stacks. Steps 44–48.

**Part IV: The back end**

- **Module 16, Packaging Fundamentals.** Backgrind, dicing, die attach, wire bond, flip-chip C4, underfill, ABF build-up substrates, leadframes, molding, BGA, and the OSATs. Steps 41–43, 49, 53–54.
- **Module 17, Advanced Packaging: CoWoS, SoIC, Chiplets.** Interposers (S/R/L), TSVs, microbumps, CoW then WoS, hybrid bonding, Foveros/EMIB, InFO, panel-level, UCIe, capacity as the AI bottleneck, warpage and thermals. Steps 50–54.
- **Module 18, Final Test, Burn-in, and System-Level Test.** Package test, burn-in, SLT, HBM KGD, fallout and cost at each stage. Steps 55–56.
- **Module 19, Building an NVIDIA GPU from RTL to Rack.** Design flow and tape-out, H100 and Blackwell anatomy, Blackwell Ultra and Rubin with HBM4, SXM, HGX, NVSwitch, DGX and GB200 NVL72, ODMs, lead times, cost breakdown. Steps 1–3 and 57–60.

**Part V: The ecosystem**

- **Module 20, Economics, Geography, and Geopolitics.** Equipment and materials oligopolies, foundry shares, fab cost curves, wafer prices by node, cost per transistor, Moore's law status, Taiwan risk, export controls, CHIPS Act, Rapidus, EU, China's domestic push, and disruption scenarios. The money-flow section of this module, at full depth.
- **Module 21, Glossary and Reference.** 150+ terms, unit conventions, a node table, the full ordered process-flow list expanded from the 60 steps above, and what to learn next.

A reading strategy that works: read Modules 00, 05, 11, 17, and 19 first for the skeleton (fab, transistor, package, product), then go back and fill in the unit processes (06–10, 12–13) and the material stages (01–04), and finish with memory (15), test (14, 18), and the ecosystem (20). If you only have a weekend, read 00, 08, 11, and 17.

## Summary

- A chip is ~100 printed layers on a 300 mm, 775 µm-thick single-crystal silicon disc; each layer is deposit → pattern → etch or implant → polish → clean and measure, and each must land on the last to within ~2 nm.
- Silicon is abundant; purity is not. Quartz at cents per kg becomes 9N–11N polysilicon at ~$20–40/kg via the Siemens route (a liquid intermediate, TCS, that can be distilled), then a single-crystal 300 mm ingot (Czochralski, ~2.5–3.5 days), then ~1,500–2,000 polished wafers at ~$100–150 each.
- The fab turns a ~$150 wafer into a ~$17,000 one over ~3 months and ~1,000–1,500 steps; ~70–80% of its ~$20–30B cost is tools, and most of a wafer's three months is spent queueing for them.
- Value and constraint both sit after the wafer: an H100 die is ~$350 of a ~$3,000 module BOM; HBM is ~40–50% of it and packaging ~20–25%; one wafer's dies become ~$1.1–1.5 million of product.
- Elapsed time is ~6–9 months from polysilicon to a shipping server; the fab is about half of it.
- Chokepoint 1: EUV. One company (ASML), ~$200–220M per tool, ~350 shipped by end-2025, a mirror-and-vacuum machine because nothing transmits 13.5 nm light, fed by a tin plasma because ~10 reflections at ~70% each leave only a few percent of the light.
- Chokepoint 2: TSMC in Taiwan makes >90% of ≤5 nm-class logic wafers because only the firm with the most customers can amortize a ~$20–30B fab: ~$5,000 of depreciation per wafer full, ~$10,000 half-empty.
- Chokepoint 3: CoWoS (~70–80k wpm end-2025, ~120–140k target end-2026) and HBM (sold out for 2025–2026 in advance) gated AI accelerator supply from 2023 through 2026, because both are new flows whose yield has to be learned.
- Japan's materials (resist, wafers, mask blanks, ABF) are a quieter fourth chokepoint, protected by qualification lock-in rather than cost.
- Seven kinds of company (EDA/IP, fabless, foundry, IDM, OSAT, equipment, materials) pass wafers and money to each other; the 1987 pure-play foundry split is why NVIDIA owns no fab.
- The 60-step master flow is the course's index; each later module expands a few of its lines to unit-process depth.

## Key Numbers

| Quantity | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|

## Common Misconceptions

- **"The chip is the expensive part of an AI GPU."** → The 814 mm² H100 die costs on the order of $350 out of a ~$3,000 bill of materials; HBM and packaging together are roughly two-thirds of it. The die is the hardest part, not the priciest.
- **"TSMC's constraint is how many wafers it can make."** → For AI accelerators, front-end wafer capacity has exceeded demand by roughly an order of magnitude; the binding constraints from 2023 to 2026 were CoWoS packaging capacity and HBM supply.
- **"A 2 nm node has 2 nm features."** → No dimension in an N2 transistor is 2 nm. Gate pitch is ~45–50 nm, metal pitch ~23–25 nm, nanosheet thickness a few nm. Node names have been marketing labels since the ~22 nm era; Module 11 explains what they actually track.
- **"A fab is a building full of robots that runs itself."** → A GIGAFAB employs several thousand engineers and technicians, and the ~3-month cycle time is dominated by queueing at ~1,000 tools, not by the processing itself. Cycle time and yield are management problems as much as physics problems.
- **"Silicon is scarce or strategically controlled."** → Quartz and MG-Si are cheap, abundant commodities. The strategic scarcity is in *purity* (electronic-grade polysilicon, HPQ crucible quartz) and in *capital and know-how* (EUV, leading-edge fabs, advanced packaging).
- **"China cannot make advanced chips because it lacks silicon or engineers."** → China dominates MG-Si and solar polysilicon and has a large engineering base. Access to some advanced equipment is constrained by export licensing, including EUV and specified immersion DUV systems. That access constraint is different from a claim that the country has no capable materials, equipment or chip suppliers. TechInsights identified SMIC’s 7 nm-class process in the commercial Kirin 9000S. A teardown establishes a manufactured device, but does not reveal a fab’s overall yield, cost or available capacity.
- **"ASML is the only EUV maker because of patents."** → Patents are the smallest part of it. EUV is a 25-year, multi-billion-euro supply chain (Zeiss optics with no second source, Trumpf lasers, the Cymer source, thousands of sub-suppliers) plus thousands of tool-years of learning about sources, mirrors and stages that exist nowhere else. A competitor holding every patent would still be a decade and tens of billions away.
- **"HBM is just DRAM chips stacked on top of each other."** → The dies are designed differently (TSV columns with keep-out zones, a 1,024- or 2,048-bit interface instead of a few dozen pins, a logic base die at the bottom), and the stacking flow is a second manufacturing process with its own bonding chemistry, yield, and test step. That is why HBM costs several times more per bit (reported 3–5x on 2023–24 contract comparisons; later estimates vary) and why only three companies make it.

## Where This Fits in the Supply Chain

This module is the map; it consumes nothing and produces the mental model every other module assumes. Module 01 picks up at the very beginning of the physical chain, where lump quartz and carbon enter a submerged arc furnace and leave as metallurgical-grade silicon on its way to a Siemens reactor. From there the chain flows in the order of the 60-step list above: polysilicon (01) to ingot (02) to wafer (03), plus the consumables and masks (04) that the fab (05–13) will burn through to turn a $150 wafer into a $17,000 one, which is sorted (14), joined to HBM (15), packaged (16–17), tested (18), and built into NVIDIA's product stack (19), inside an industry structure whose economics and geography are analyzed in Module 20. The reference material in Module 21 closes the loop by expanding this module's process flow to full granularity.

# Module 01: Sand to Polysilicon

This stage has a clear goal: take silicon dioxide, the most abundant compound in the Earth's crust, and turn it into elemental silicon in which fewer than one atom in a billion is anything other than silicon.

The amount of silicon is not the difficulty. The difficulty is controlling which foreign atoms remain among its atoms, because different impurities change electrical behaviour in different ways. A **dopant** is an impurity added on purpose: boron has one electron fewer than silicon and makes **p-type** silicon, in which current is carried by mobile electron vacancies called holes; phosphorus has one electron more and makes **n-type** silicon, in which current is carried by the spare electrons. A transistor uses carefully arranged regions of semiconductor to control current, so the wafer maker introduces a controlled dopant concentration of perhaps 10^15 atoms per cm³ and needs any residual, uncontrolled boron and phosphorus to be at least a thousand times lower than that. Boron and phosphorus are dangerous precisely because they are dopants: a stray one changes the switch's behaviour.

Metals cause a different problem: an atom of iron, copper, or nickel lodged in the lattice acts as a trap that swallows the free electrons the switch relies on, or as a short through the **gate oxide**, the insulating layer only a few atoms thick that separates the silicon from the transistor's control electrode (its **gate**, the terminal whose voltage turns the switch on and off).

The product of this stage is **polycrystalline silicon (polysilicon)**: a solid made of millions of small silicon crystals in random orientations, which is what you get when silicon deposits everywhere at once on a hot rod. A wafer needs one continuous crystal; turning polysilicon into that is Module 02's job.

Nature does not hand out silicon in that condition. The Si-O bond is one of the strongest in geochemistry (~450 kJ/mol per bond, stronger than the carbon-carbon single bond that holds a hydrocarbon chain together (~350 kJ/mol) and a little stronger than a C-H bond (~410 kJ/mol), and every silicon in quartz has four of them), which is why quartz survives billions of years of weathering, and it is why breaking it costs a submerged-arc furnace (an electric furnace, Section 3) running at ~2,000 °C and roughly 12 MWh of electricity per tonne. The silicon that comes out of that furnace is ~98–99% pure, which is fine for aluminum alloys and silicones and hopeless for a wafer (Section 6 defines the grades). Going from 99% to 99.9999999% (nine nines, or **9N**) is a chemistry problem, not a metallurgy problem: convert the silicon into a volatile liquid, distill the liquid until the contaminants are at parts-per-trillion levels, and then decompose the liquid back into solid silicon inside a sealed reactor at ~1,100 °C. That is the **Siemens process**, invented at Siemens in the late 1950s and still, seven decades later, the way essentially all electronic-grade silicon is made.

This module walks the full chain: the rock, the furnace, the chlorosilane chemistry, the deposition reactor, the competing fluidized-bed route, how purity is actually measured, how **chunks** (the fist-sized broken pieces of rod in which polysilicon ships) get to a crystal grower, who makes what, and what it costs. It closes with the two other ultra-pure feedstocks that enter the supply chain at this same stage and that the crystal grower in Module 02 cannot work without: the fused-quartz crucible and the graphite hot zone.

## Before you start

- **Atoms, moles and Avogadro's number.** One mole is 6.022 × 10^23 particles, and an element's atomic mass in grams is one mole of its atoms, so a solid's density tells you how many atoms sit in a cubic centimetre; this module counts impurities that way.
- **Parts-per notation.** ppm, ppb and ppt are parts per million, billion and trillion. Counting by weight (ppmw, ppbw) and by atoms (ppma, ppba, ppta) give different numbers for the same sample, because atoms of different elements weigh different amounts.
- **Crystal, polycrystal, glass.** A **single crystal** is one continuous, ordered lattice; a **polycrystal** is many small crystals (grains) in random orientations; a **glass** (an amorphous solid) has no long-range order. This module makes polycrystals and uses glass (fused quartz) to hold molten silicon; Module 02 makes single crystals.
- **Dopants and resistivity.** Boron (one electron fewer than silicon) makes p-type silicon; phosphorus (one more) makes n-type. More dopant means more mobile charge carriers and lower **resistivity**, measured in ohm-centimetres (Ω·cm). Module 10 goes deep.
- **Heat of reaction.** A reaction's enthalpy change ΔH is the heat it absorbs (positive) or releases (negative). Its entropy change ΔS describes the change in how widely matter and energy can be distributed; producing gas often increases it. The balance is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is absolute temperature in kelvin and ΔG is the Gibbs free-energy change. A negative ΔG says the reaction is thermodynamically favoured under the stated conditions. It does not say how fast it happens; temperature must also make the reaction fast enough to be useful.
- **Boiling points and distillation.** Liquids with different boiling points can be separated by boiling and condensing, because the vapour is richer in the lower-boiling component. Doing that once is school chemistry; this module explains how a column does it a hundred times over.
- **Thermal radiation.** Every hot surface radiates power proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature (the Stefan-Boltzmann law, Section 4.3). At 1,100 °C this dwarfs every other heat loss.
- **Units.** 1 MWh = 1,000 kWh; 1 bar is roughly atmospheric pressure; 1 tonne (t) = 1,000 kg, 1 kt = 1,000 t, 1 Mt = a million tonnes; 1 µm is a thousandth of a millimetre. Temperatures are in °C except where a T⁴ law needs kelvin (K = °C + 273).
- **The chain (Module 00).** Quartz → metallurgical silicon → polysilicon → single crystal (an **ingot**, a cylindrical log of one crystal) → **wafer** (a thin disc sliced from it) → fab. This module covers the first two arrows, plus the crucible and graphite the third arrow needs.

## 1. Why Purity Is the Whole Game

Crystalline silicon contains **5.0 × 10^22 atoms per cm³** (density 2.33 g/cm³, atomic mass 28.09 g/mol; 2.33 / 28.09 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 4.99 × 10^22). A cubic centimetre is a sugar cube, and one part per billion of that sugar cube is still fifty trillion atoms. That number is the yardstick for everything in this module, so it is worth internalizing.

Purity for semiconductor silicon is usually quoted in "nines": 6N is 99.9999% (1 part per million impurity), 9N is 99.9999999% (1 part per billion), 11N is 99.999999999% (10 parts per trillion). Because the interesting impurities are counted as atoms, the industry uses **ppma** (parts per million atomic), **ppba** (parts per billion atomic) and **ppta** (parts per trillion atomic) for dopants, and **ppbw** (parts per billion by weight) for metals, which are usually measured by **mass spectrometry** (an instrument that turns the atoms in a sample into charged ions and sorts them by mass, so that each element is counted separately; Section 7 describes the version the industry uses) after dissolving the sample. The conversion matters: 1 ppbw of iron (atomic mass 56) is 0.5 ppba, because an iron atom weighs twice a silicon atom.

Three more definitions before the arithmetic. **Resistivity**, in ohm-centimetres (Ω·cm), is how hard it is to push current through a 1 cm cube of the material; more dopant atoms mean more carriers and lower resistivity, so wafer makers quote dopant content as a resistivity rather than as a count. **Czochralski (CZ)** growth pulls a single crystal out of a melt held in a crucible; **float-zone (FZ)** growth melts a rod one short zone at a time, using a **radio-frequency (RF) induction coil** and no crucible at all, so nothing but the feedstock's own impurities enters the crystal (Module 02 covers both). The coil is a water-cooled copper ring, a few turns wide, carrying alternating current at ~MHz frequency; its rapidly reversing magnetic field induces circulating currents in the silicon inside the ring, and those currents heat the silicon by its own resistance, so the coil melts a slice of the rod without ever touching it, like an induction hob heating a pan. And an impurity is **electrically active** if it dopes: boron, aluminum, gallium (one column to the left of silicon in the periodic table) each remove one electron, and phosphorus, arsenic, antimony (one column to the right) each contribute one, so every one of their atoms changes the resistivity. Iron and copper do not dope; they trap.

> **Worked example: what 9N means in atoms.**
> Silicon has 5 × 10^22 atoms per cm³. A total impurity content of 1 ppb (9N) means 5 × 10^22 × 10^-9 = **5 × 10^13 impurity atoms per cm³**. That sounds like a lot of atoms (fifty trillion in a sugar-cube volume), but compare it to the dopants a wafer maker adds on purpose. A standard p-type 300 mm CZ substrate (the wafer as a physical base for transistors) at ~10 Ω·cm has about 1.3 × 10^15 boron atoms per cm³ (about 27 ppba; the conversion from resistivity to atom count comes from the standard published resistivity-to-dopant curves, SEMI MF723, and Section 7 explains how the resistivity itself is measured). So a 9N feedstock carries roughly 25× fewer total foreign atoms than the deliberate doping level, and the fraction that is electrically active (B, P, Al, As, Sb) is far lower still. The electronic-grade specification for boron is typically ≤ ~0.02–0.05 ppba, i.e. ≤ 1–2.5 × 10^12 atoms per cm³, a thousand times below the intentional dopant level. At the other end, a 6N solar feedstock whose entire 1 ppm impurity budget were boron (a worst case; real 6N silicon carries a mix of impurities, but it makes the scale clear) would contain 5 × 10^16 boron atoms per cm³, giving a resistivity of ~0.3–0.5 Ω·cm before the grower adds anything at all; that is why 6N is a solar number and not an electronics number. And a high-resistivity float-zone wafer for radio-frequency or power devices at 5,000 Ω·cm needs net electrically active impurities below ~3 × 10^12 atoms per cm³, which is only reachable because the feedstock's boron and phosphorus are each at the 10^11–10^12 atoms per cm³ level.

> **Intuition:** sea ice is fresher than the sea it froze from, because the orderly ice lattice has no room for salt ions and pushes them back into the water. Freezing silicon does the same thing. A misfit atom such as iron or copper, the wrong size and with the wrong bonding habits, is shoved into the liquid as the crystal front advances. Boron is different: it is small, it bonds to four neighbours the way silicon does, and it fits into a silicon lattice site almost comfortably, so the crystal accepts most of it. The analogy breaks only in degree: sea ice rejects salt by a factor of a few, while silicon rejects iron by a factor of a hundred thousand.

That picture is quantified by the **segregation coefficient** k of each impurity: the ratio of its concentration in the freshly frozen solid to its concentration in the liquid it froze from. Iron has k ≈ 8 × 10^-6, aluminum ~2 × 10^-3, copper ~4 × 10^-4: crystal growth rejects them into the melt almost completely, so a polysilicon feedstock can tolerate a little metal that the grower will clean up. Carbon has k ≈ 0.07, so a tenth of it stays. Oxygen is a special case: the feedstock carries almost none, and the crucible adds it during growth (Section 10 and Module 02). Boron has k ≈ 0.8 and phosphorus k ≈ 0.35. Boron in particular goes straight into the crystal. It cannot be removed by crystal growth, by **zone refining** (sweeping a molten zone along a rod so that impurities that prefer the liquid ride along to the end), or by any metallurgical trick with reasonable yield. It has to be removed at the chemical stage, in the distillation columns, and that single fact shapes the design of the entire Siemens process.

> **Worked example: one freezing pass.**
> The rule is reusable: the first solid to freeze carries k times the melt concentration. For boron, k ≈ 0.8, so the crystal keeps ~80% of what was in the melt (and as the melt shrinks and its boron concentrates, later parts of the crystal carry even more). For iron, k ≈ 10^-5, so the crystal keeps one part in a hundred thousand: a melt at 1 ppm of iron gives a crystal at ~10 ppt. One pass of crystal growth is a superb iron filter and a useless boron filter.

> **Why it matters downstream:** the boron in the feedstock sets a floor under everything grown from it. A float-zone wafer for a radio-frequency switch or a high-voltage power device needs several thousand Ω·cm, which means boron and phosphorus at the 10^11–10^12 atoms per cm³ level, and downstream steps are not a substitute for a qualified low-impurity feedstock. Crystal segregation can redistribute impurities, and zone refining can remove some; neither makes feedstock purity irrelevant.

## 2. The Rock: Quartz and Quartzite

### 2.1 Why not beach sand

Start with why the furnace cares about the shape of its rock. The reaction in Section 3 strips both oxygens off every silicon atom and turns them into two molecules of carbon monoxide gas, and that gas has to escape upward through a pile of rock and coal several metres deep (the **charge**, the batch of raw materials loaded into the furnace, which sits as a **packed bed**, a heap of lumps with gas-filled gaps between them). If the pile is not porous, the gas does not leave quietly. The "sand to chip" phrase is a nice story and it is essentially wrong. Beach and desert sand is a poor feedstock for three reasons, all of them mechanistic.

First, grain size. Fine sand (0.1–1 mm) packs into an impermeable mass. The trapped gas then either **channels** (finds one path and blasts through it, leaving the rest of the pile unreacted) or **blows** (a pocket of trapped gas erupts through the surface), and the furnace becomes unstable and dangerous. Furnaces need lumpy material, typically **10–150 mm** pieces, with fines screened out.

Second, chemistry. Beach sand contains shell fragments (CaCO₃), heavy minerals (ilmenite FeTiO₃, zircon, monazite, magnetite), feldspar (Al, Na, K), and clay. Iron, aluminum, titanium, calcium, and especially boron and phosphorus (from apatite, tourmaline, and organic residues) all end up in the silicon. Boron and phosphorus are the ones the downstream chemistry hates most.

Third, thermal behavior. At 573 °C the atoms in quartz snap from one arrangement (α-quartz) into a slightly different one (β-quartz), with an abrupt volume jump of roughly 1%; a lump heated quickly cracks along the front where that jump is happening. Some quartz **decrepitates** (shatters into fines) on rapid heating through that transition and again near its ~1,700 °C softening point, which recreates the permeability problem inside the furnace. Producers test candidate ore for **thermal strength** and pick deposits that stay lumpy.

So the furnace feed is **lump quartz** or **quartzite** (a metamorphosed quartz sandstone) mined from hard-rock quarries, crushed and screened to size, and specified at roughly ≥ 98–99.5% SiO₂, with Fe₂O₃ and Al₂O₃ each in the 0.05–0.5% range, and B and P in the low-ppm range. Major sources are Norway, Spain, France, Brazil, Canada, Australia, South Africa, Turkey, and many quarries in China. A silicon smelter uses ~2.5–2.7 tonnes of quartz per tonne of silicon. The theoretical figure is 2.14: SiO₂ weighs 60.08 g/mol and silicon 28.09 g/mol, and 60.08 / 28.09 = 2.14. The rest is lost as silica fume (Section 3.1) and **slag**, a molten oxide layer that floats on liquid metal and carries away the oxides you want gone.

> **Worked example: how much boron a quarry delivers.**
> Suppose a quartz lot carries 10 ppm of boron by weight, at the top of the "low-ppm" specification. At 2.5–2.7 t of quartz per tonne of silicon, that is ~25–27 g of boron per tonne of silicon. If all of it stayed, the silicon would contain ~25 ppmw of boron, squarely inside the 5–40 ppmw measured in real metallurgical silicon (Section 3.3); in practice some boron leaves with the fume and the coal ash adds some back. The point stands: whatever boron the quarry delivers, the chlorosilane plant in Section 4 must remove, and nothing in the furnace will do it for you.

### 2.2 High-purity quartz: a different material for a different job

There is a second quartz stream in the supply chain, and it is much rarer, much more expensive, and much more geographically concentrated. **High-purity quartz (HPQ)** is quartz with total impurities below roughly 50 ppm, in the best grades below ~10 ppm, with particular attention to aluminum, titanium, and the alkalis (Na, K, Li). These sit inside the quartz lattice as **substitutional** ions (taking a silicon atom's place) or **interstitial** ions (squeezed into a gap between atoms), and cannot be washed off. HPQ is not fed to furnaces. It is the raw material for the **fused-quartz crucibles** in which single crystals are grown (Section 10 and Module 02), for quartz furnace tubes and wafer boats, for lamp envelopes, and for the silica used in some optical and telecom applications. A crucible cares about those particular impurities for a concrete reason: alkalis make the glass flow and crystallize at melt temperature, aluminum and titanium dissolve into the melt and end up in the crystal, and any of them weakens the bubble-free inner layer that keeps the crucible from shedding particles (Section 10.1).

The world's benchmark deposit is the **Spruce Pine** pegmatite district in Mitchell County, North Carolina. A **pegmatite** is a very coarse-grained igneous rock; this one is an alaskite (a feldspar-quartz-mica granite) in which the quartz crystallized unusually clean of trace elements, and which, crucially, can be liberated from the feldspar and mica by crushing, froth flotation, magnetic separation, and acid leaching. Two companies mine it: **Sibelco** (Belgian, whose Spruce Pine operation descends from Unimin and sells the IOTA family of grades; IOTA-STD is on the order of 20 ppm total impurities, ~14 ppm of it aluminum, and the premium grades, IOTA-4 and above and the crucible-optimized IOTA-CG, bring the total down to roughly 8–10 ppm, with aluminum at ~8 ppm, the floor the geology sets; Section 10.1 and the Key Numbers table reuse these figures) and **The Quartz Corp** (a joint venture of Norway's Norsk Mineral and France's Imerys), which mines at Spruce Pine and does its final purification at Drag in northern Norway. Between them they supply the large majority of the world's crucible-grade quartz, and in the tightest grades effectively all of it. Other HPQ sources exist but are second-tier or politically awkward: Kyshtym in Russia's Urals (sanctions-affected), deposits in India, Brazil, Australia, Mauritania, and China's Donghai county in Jiangsu, home of Jiangsu Pacific Quartz, the Chinese leader in both natural HPQ processing and synthetic quartz.

The purification flowsheet defines the price:

1. **Crush** the rock to sand-sized grains, so that each grain is mostly one mineral and the quartz can be separated from the feldspar and mica physically.
2. **Float**: **froth flotation** adds chemicals that make one mineral's surface water-repellent, so that air bubbles blown through the slurry carry it to the top; this rejects feldspar and mica.
3. **Magnetic separation** at high field strength pulls out iron-bearing minerals, which are weakly magnetic.
4. **Acid leach** in hot hydrochloric and hydrofluoric acid dissolves the impurities sitting on grain surfaces and along grain boundaries.
5. **Hot chlorination**, for the top grades only: the sand is heated to ~1,000–1,200 °C in chlorine or HCl gas, which converts alkalis near the lattice surface and some aluminum and iron into volatile chlorides that boil away.

What remains is dominated by aluminum substituting for silicon deep in the lattice, which no step removes; that is why the geology matters more than the plant.

### 2.3 The Hurricane Helene scare

A side note, because it is the episode most readers will have heard of. On 26–27 September 2024 Hurricane Helene dumped historic rainfall on western North Carolina, destroying Spruce Pine's roads, rail spur, power and water; both Sibelco and The Quartz Corp had halted operations ahead of the storm, and for about two weeks the press ran the headline that the world's chip supply depended on one flattened mountain town. Sibelco announced production and shipments restarting on 10 October 2024; The Quartz Corp resumed later, as the local infrastructure was rebuilt, without publishing a single restart date. Three things kept the scare from becoming a shortage: crucible and wafer makers hold months of HPQ inventory precisely because the source is concentrated, and quartz does not degrade in a warehouse; the mines themselves were intact, the damage being to the town and its transport links; and a crucible needs ultra-clean quartz only in its inner few millimetres, for which synthetic quartz (Section 10.1) is a qualified if pricier substitute. The lasting effect was to accelerate second-source qualification of Chinese synthetic quartz and alternative natural deposits; the episode is now the standard example of a single point of failure that is neither a chip nor a tool.

## 3. Carbothermic Reduction: The Submerged-Arc Furnace

### 3.1 The chemistry

The overall reaction is

SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO

with ΔH ≈ +690 kJ per mole of silicon. That number comes from **formation enthalpies**, the heat released when a compound forms from its elements: SiO₂ releases 911 kJ/mol when it forms, CO releases 110.5 kJ/mol, and the reaction's ΔH is the products' total minus the reactants', 2 × (−110.5) − (−911) = +690 kJ/mol. The positive sign means heat must be supplied: the reaction is strongly **endothermic**. It is electric rather than fuel-fired for a simple reason: no flame can hold the required temperature inside a bed of carbon that would consume the flame's oxygen.

> **Intuition:** picture a pit ~10 m across filled with quartz lumps and coal, with three carbon columns as thick as tree trunks plunged into it from above. Around each column tip the electric arc hollows out a gas-filled cavity (the **crater**) at ~2,000 °C, and the pile above the crater is cooler the higher you go. Gas rises, solids sink, so the furnace is a counter-current trap: half-finished product rising as gas must be caught by the carbon it meets on the way up and dragged back down as a solid. The half-finished product is **silicon monoxide, SiO(g)** (the "(g)" means gas), a molecule that exists only at these temperatures. Any that escapes the trap is lost.

> **Worked example: why 2,000 °C.**
> Whether a reaction goes is decided by the Gibbs free energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where ΔH is the heat absorbed (+690,000 J per mole of silicon here), T is the absolute temperature in kelvin, and ΔS is the entropy change, the gain in disorder. This reaction turns two solids into a solid plus two molecules of gas, and gas is far more disordered than solid. Using the standard-table entropies: the two moles of CO gas made carry 2 × 198 ≈ 395 J/K; subtract the ~53 J/K that the solids consumed had (quartz ~42 J/K per mole, plus two moles of carbon at ~6 J/K each); add the ~19 J/K of the mole of solid silicon made; net ΔS ≈ 395 − 53 + 19 ≈ **+360 J per mole of silicon per kelvin**. The reaction becomes favourable when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. above T ≈ 690,000 / 360 ≈ 1,900 K, about 1,650 °C, for the overall equation. That is an estimated crossing using constant standard-state enthalpy and entropy, not a rigorous furnace-equilibrium temperature. The furnace runs hotter because the overall equation never happens in one step: the final step that actually makes liquid silicon, SiO(g) + SiC → 2Si + CO(g) below, needs the crater at or above ~1,800 °C to run at a useful rate, which is why the hot zone sits at ~1,900–2,000 °C and no hotter, since every degree of margin costs power and quartz.

The real chemistry is staged, and understanding the stages explains most of the furnace's design and most of its losses. In the hot crater around each electrode tip:

SiO₂ + C → SiO(g) + CO(g)
SiO₂ + Si → 2SiO(g)
SiO(g) + SiC → 2Si + CO(g)

Higher up in the bed, where the charge is cooler (~1,500–1,800 °C), the rising silicon monoxide gas is captured by the carbon:

SiO(g) + 2C → SiC + CO(g)

and the silicon carbide then descends into the crater to be consumed by the third reaction above. In other words, silicon carbide is the working intermediate, and gaseous SiO is the carrier that has to be trapped on its way up. Any SiO that reaches the top of the charge oxidizes in air to a cloud of **amorphous** (glass-like, with no crystal order) SiO₂ nanoparticles called **silica fume** or microsilica, which is bag-filtered and sold to the concrete industry. For the stated 2.5–2.7 t quartz feed, a simple balance assuming pure SiO₂ gives 2.139/(2.5–2.7), or about 79–86% recovery of feed silicon into metal. Industrial yield figures can use different feed and recycle boundaries; they should not be equated automatically with this balance. Unrecovered silicon includes material in fume and slag. A furnace that is run too hot, too fast, or with too little reactive carbon in the upper bed loses more.

### 3.2 The furnace

A modern silicon furnace is a steel shell lined with **refractory** (a ceramic that stays solid and inert at very high temperature), typically 8–12 m in diameter and several meters deep, open at the top (or fitted with a semi-closed hood for gas capture), rated at **10–45 MW**. Three **Söderberg electrodes**, self-baking carbon columns 1.2–2 m in diameter, hang from above and descend into the charge. Söderberg electrodes are made continuously: a steel casing is filled with carbon paste (anthracite, a hard coal, plus coal-tar pitch, a tarry binder) at the top, and as the column is slipped downward the paste bakes into solid electrode in the heat of the furnace. The three electrodes carry **three-phase alternating current** (the standard form of heavy industrial power: three alternating currents, one per electrode, offset from one another by a third of a cycle, so that at every instant current is flowing through the charge between some pair of electrodes) at low voltage and enormous current, and the tips sit in gas-filled craters below the charge surface, hence "submerged arc." The numbers: a 40 MW furnace splits its power roughly three ways, ~13 MW per electrode, and the voltage between electrode and **hearth** (the furnace floor, a carbon-lined basin on which the molten silicon pools) is only ~100–150 V because the charge and the arc offer little resistance, so the current is 13,000,000 W / ~130 V ≈ 100 kA per electrode. A domestic kettle draws ~10 A; one Söderberg column carries the current of ten thousand kettles, which is why it is a metre or two thick and why the busbars (the heavy conductors feeding it) are water-cooled copper. The heat is a mixture of arc and resistive heating through the charge and the molten silicon. Electrode consumption is on the order of 100 kg per tonne of silicon and is itself a carbon input to the reaction.

The charge is dosed by weight from bins: quartz lumps plus a carefully balanced reductant mix. The reductants are chosen for **reactivity toward SiO** (how well they capture the gas on the way up), for **porosity** (a permeable charge that lets gas out and heat in), and for **ash chemistry** (ash is the mineral residue left when carbon burns, and it is where the Fe, Al, Ca, Ti, B, and P come from). The typical mix is:

- **Coal**, usually low-ash bituminous (ordinary soft) coal from Colombia or similar, the main carbon source;
- **Charcoal**, more reactive and lower in ash than coal, especially valued in Brazil and Norway, and the reason some smelters advertise a partly renewable carbon footprint;
- **Petroleum coke**, the dense, low-ash carbon left over from oil refining, low in reactivity and used sparingly;
- **Wood chips**, which contribute little carbon but keep the charge open and porous, prevent crusting, and improve SiO capture in the upper bed. A smelter consumes wood chips by the truckload, on the order of ~1 t of chips per tonne of silicon (an order-of-magnitude figure that varies with the recipe), and a shortage of clean, dry chips is a real operating constraint.

The furnace is stoked continuously: a stoking machine (or, in older plants, workers with long steel poles) breaks the crust that forms at the surface, pushes fresh charge toward the electrodes, and keeps the craters from collapsing. Molten silicon (melting point 1,414 °C) pools on the hearth and is **tapped** every 1–2 hours: a tap hole in the side wall is opened with an oxygen lance or a drilling machine, the liquid metal runs out, and the hole is closed again with a clay plug.

> **What can go wrong:** the furnace is a slow, hot, partly blind process, and most of its failure modes are about the bed. A hard **crust** of sintered charge (lumps fused together by heat without melting) and condensed SiO forms at the surface and traps gas beneath it until it **blows**, an eruption of hot gas and charge that can injure the stoking crew; the cure is more wood chips and more stoking. An electrode whose paste baked too fast or too slowly cracks, a metre or more of it drops into the crater, and the furnace loses a third of its power for days while the column is re-baked and lowered. Silicon carbide accumulates on the hearth if the bed is too carbon-rich, raising the furnace bottom until the electrodes cannot form a proper crater; the remedy is to run "under-coked" for a while to consume it. The tap hole blocks with SiC and slag and must be lanced open. And a quartz lot high in boron or titanium cannot be fixed by anything at the smelter, so tap chemistry drifts until the lot is used up. Operators read the bed through electrode position and electrical resistance (a rising electrode means a shrinking crater), off-gas temperature and fume rate, and the chemistry of every tap.

### 3.3 Refining, casting, crushing

The liquid silicon runs into a **ladle** (a large refractory-lined bucket), where it is **oxidatively refined**: a mixture of oxygen and air is blown through the melt beneath a lime-silica slag (Section 2.1: a molten oxide layer floating on the metal that absorbs the oxides you want gone). Which elements the oxygen removes is set by their appetite for oxygen, which runs Ca > Al > Si > Fe. Aluminum and calcium oxidize preferentially (their oxides are more stable than SiO₂) and **report to the slag**, the metallurgist's phrase for "end up in the slag layer rather than in the metal"; a typical refining step takes Al from ~0.5% to ~0.1% and Ca from ~0.3% to below ~0.05%. Iron is not removed by this step, because Fe is more **noble** than Si (less eager to grab oxygen), so blowing oxygen would burn silicon before it touched the iron; iron control therefore has to be done at the raw-material end. Boron and phosphorus are essentially untouched by ladle refining.

The refined silicon is cast into shallow iron or graphite moulds, or onto a casting bed, as slabs ~10 cm thick. Slow cooling segregates the remaining Fe, Al, Ca, and Ti into **intermetallic** phases (compounds of two or more metals with their own crystal structure, here FeSi₂ and Al-Ca-Si compounds) at the **grain boundaries**, the surfaces where neighbouring silicon crystals meet. This matters later: the intermetallics react with HCl at a different rate from silicon and their aluminum and calcium can shift the product split in the fluidized bed of Section 4.1, which is why some polysilicon makers specify the cooling rate and grain structure of the silicon they buy (practice varies by plant, and the effect is second-order next to the boron and phosphorus content). The slabs are crushed to the customer's size, typically 10–100 mm lumps for chemical customers.

The product is **metallurgical-grade silicon (MG-Si)**, also called silicon metal, at **98.5–99.5% Si**. A representative analysis: Fe 0.2–0.6%, Al 0.1–0.4%, Ca 0.02–0.2%, Ti 0.01–0.05%, B 5–40 ppmw, P 10–50 ppmw, plus carbon at saturation (a few hundred ppm as dissolved C and SiC). Polysilicon makers specify a "chemical grade" with tighter limits, especially on Ti, B, and P, and pay a premium for it.

> **Worked example: energy and efficiency of the arc furnace.**
> The reaction enthalpy is +690 kJ per mole of Si, and one mole is 28.09 g, so the simplified reaction-enthalpy requirement is 690 / 28.09 = 24.6 MJ/kg = 6.8 kWh/kg, or **6.8 MWh per tonne** of silicon, before counting the energy to heat the reactants to 2,000 °C, the latent heat of melting (the heat needed to melt a solid without raising its temperature), and the heat carried out by ~2 tonnes of CO gas per tonne of Si. Real furnaces consume **11–13 MWh/tonne** (the best large furnaces are near 11; small or old ones exceed 13), so the reaction-to-electricity efficiency is on the order of 55–60%, which for a 2,000 °C high-temperature process is respectable. At an industrial electricity price of $0.05/kWh, the power bill alone is ~$600/tonne, roughly a quarter to a third of the ~$1,500–2,500/tonne price of chemical-grade MG-Si (Chinese domestic prices at the low end, Western contract prices at the high end, as of 2025); that arithmetic is why silicon smelters cluster where hydro (Norway, Quebec, Yunnan, Sichuan) or cheap coal (Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia) power sits. The CO₂ footprint from the carbon reductant alone is ~4–5 tonnes CO₂ per tonne Si, and it can be built up in three steps. **Stoichiometry** (the fixed atom ratios of the balanced equation) says two moles of carbon per mole of silicon: 2 × 12.01 g of carbon per 28.09 g of silicon, i.e. 0.855 t of carbon per tonne of silicon. Every 12 g of carbon becomes 44 g of CO₂ once the CO burns in the off-gas (CO₂ carries two oxygens of 16 g each), so the stoichiometric minimum is 0.855 t × (44 / 12) = 3.1 t of CO₂ per tonne of silicon. Real furnaces use more carbon than that: ~1.2 t of **fixed carbon** per tonne of silicon, where fixed carbon is the carbon left in coal, charcoal or coke after its moisture and volatile matter (tars and gases) are driven off, i.e. the part that actually reacts (ordinary coal is only ~55–70% fixed carbon, which is why a smelter's coal tonnage is larger than these figures). The excess over 0.855 t goes to the SiO that escapes as fume after carbon was spent making it, and to the electrode paste, which is a carbon input too. So the real footprint is 1.2 t × (44 / 12) = 4.4 t of CO₂ per tonne of silicon.

### 3.4 Who makes MG-Si

Global silicon-metal production is on the order of 4.5–5 million tonnes a year, and China produces roughly 80–85% of it; the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries put 2024 world output at ~4.6 Mt with Chinese output at ~3.9 Mt (USGS counts silicon content; Chinese industry data, which count gross tonnage and include **secondary silicon**, scrap and off-grade silicon re-melted and resold rather than freshly smelted, run higher). The largest single producer is **Hoshine Silicon** in Xinjiang, with well over a million tonnes of capacity. Outside China, **Ferroglobe** (Spain, France, Canada, the US, South Africa; ~350 kt/yr silicon-metal nameplate, with actual output lower in 2024–25) and **Elkem** (Norway, Iceland, Canada, Paraguay, China; Norwegian-listed and majority owned by China National Bluestar) dominate, with **Dow** (Brazil), **RIMA** and **Liasa** (Brazil), **Simcoa** (Australia), and **Mississippi Silicon** (US) as smaller players.
