Substrate strips (BGAs) and MAP-molded leadframe strips (QFNs) are **sawn** apart; QFPs and other leaded parts go through **trim and form** instead: a die punch cuts the dam bars and lead tips free of the strip and bends the leads into gull wings, after which the parts are checked optically for lead coplanarity, the ~0.1 mm specification from the Leadframes section.

Package sawing is wafer dicing made coarse. The strip is mounted on UV dicing tape on a frame, or clamped in a vacuum **jig** (a machined plate with a pocket for each unit, which holds every package after the cuts free it), and a **package saw** (Disco again, with its DFD-series machines; also Tokyo Seimitsu and others) cuts along the saw streets between units. The blade is a resin-bond diamond blade, roughly five to ten times thicker than a wafer hub blade (of order ~0.2–0.3 mm, an estimate, against 20–50 µm), with coarser diamonds, because it must cut through ~0.2–0.5 mm of copper leadframe or copper-and-glass-fiber substrate plus the epoxy body, materials that are gummy (copper), abrasive (glass fiber) and hard (silica-filled EMC) at once; the blade wears far faster than on silicon and is dressed and replaced on a shorter schedule. The kerf is correspondingly ~0.2–0.3 mm and the saw streets on a QFN strip ~0.3 mm, a design cost of a few percent of the strip's area. Spindles run slower than for wafers, tens of thousands of rpm, and feeds are of order ~50–100 mm/s (estimates; recipes are per product), so a strip carrying a few hundred QFNs is cut in a minute or two, and dual-spindle saws cut two streets at once. QFN strips are usually cut from the leadframe side so that the blade enters the copper first and the burr it raises is pushed into the mold body rather than dragged across the solderable pads. After sawing, the units are washed to remove the copper- and epoxy-laden cutting slurry, dried, and picked from the tape or jig by a **sorter** with vision inspection of both faces.

> **What can go wrong (singulation):** **Copper burrs**: the blade smears copper along the cut edge of a QFN's pads and leads; a burr can bridge two adjacent pads or stand proud and block solder wetting, and it is the singulation defect the industry fights hardest, by cut direction, blade choice and feed rate. **Mold-to-leadframe delamination** starting at the cut edge, where the blade's side load pries the epoxy off the smooth copper, which later becomes a moisture path and a popcorning site. **Mold chipping** at the package edge and top corners, cosmetic in itself but a crack starter. **Blade loading and wear**: copper clogs a resin-bond blade, the cut heats, and chipping and burrs rise together; the fix is dressing and a metered blade life. **Cut-position error**: a saw street that drifts by a fraction of its width cuts into a BGA's outer ball pads or a QFN's leads. **Pop-off**: a unit lifts from the tape or jig mid-cut and is destroyed. **Die crack** in very thin packages clamped too hard. Detection is optical inspection of every unit's edges and pads after sorting, and the fix is almost always blade, feed or mounting rather than the saw.

Finished units are loaded into **JEDEC trays** (standardized plastic trays with a pocket per unit, for larger packages) or onto **tape-and-reel** (a pocketed plastic carrier tape with a peel-off cover, wound on a reel, the way pick-and-place machines on a board assembly line are fed) and move to package-level test, **burn-in** (running the parts hot and at elevated voltage for hours to force early-life failures to show themselves before shipment) and system-level test, the subject of Module 18. Assembly yield at an OSAT for a mature FCBGA is typically 99%+; each 1% of loss at this stage destroys dies worth more than the entire assembly cost, which is why known-good-die testing (Module 14) matters.

## Wafer-Level and Fan-Out Packaging

Two definitions first. **Fan-in** means the package's terminals stay inside the die's own footprint; **fan-out** means the wiring extends past the die edge onto surrounding material, so a small die can carry more terminals than fit on its face. Both replace the substrate with a **redistribution layer (RDL)**: thin copper wiring built directly on the die (or on the die plus its surroundings) by fab-style lithography, insulated by **polyimide** or **PBO** (polybenzoxazole), heat-resistant polymers spun on as a liquid and patterned like resist.

**Wafer-level chip-scale packaging (WLCSP)** is the fan-in case and skips the substrate entirely. On the finished wafer, a polymer dielectric is spun and patterned, a sputtered-and-plated copper RDL re-routes the peripheral pads into an area array, a second polymer layer defines UBM openings, and solder balls of ~0.2–0.3 mm at 0.35–0.5 mm pitch are dropped and reflowed directly on the die. After backgrinding, a backside laminate protects the silicon, and the wafer is diced. The package is exactly the die size; a die can only carry as many balls as fit on its own area. WLCSP dominates for PMICs (the regulators that make the dozen voltages a phone needs), RF front-end parts and small sensors in phones (hundreds per phone); the lines that run it are the bumping lines described in Step 1 with an extra polymer-and-RDL layer, at the big OSATs (ASE, Amkor, JCET, PTI) and at the bumping houses of the foundries. Its Achilles' heel is the CTE problem: a 5 mm bare silicon die soldered straight to an **FR-4** board (the standard glass-epoxy board material, CTE ~17 ppm/K) survives temperature cycling only because it is small (short DNP); WLCSPs above ~6–7 mm are rare for exactly this reason.

> **Intuition:** fan-out is re-potting a plant. The die is the root ball; it is set into a bigger pot of mold compound, and the wiring, like roots, can then spread beyond the original ball into the new soil. Where the picture breaks: the new soil (epoxy) and the root ball (silicon) expand differently, and the roots (RDL copper) must cross the boundary between them at every die edge.

**Fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP)** removes the die-size limit. Infineon's **eWLB** (embedded wafer-level BGA, 2006, later licensed to STATS ChipPAC/JCET, Nanium/Amkor and ASE) established the flow:

1. Dice the wafer; place good dies face-down on a carrier coated with a **thermal-release tape** (an adhesive that holds at room temperature and lets go when heated past a set point, so the carrier can be removed later without solvents), spaced further apart than they were on the original wafer.
2. Compression-mold EMC over the dies (Molding section) to form a **reconstituted wafer**: a 300 mm disc of epoxy with the dies embedded in it (or a rectangular panel in panel-level variants).
3. Debond the carrier, exposing the die faces flush with the mold surface.
4. Build RDL layers across both die and mold, fanning connections out beyond the die edge. Each layer is ~3–5 µm of copper in ~5–10 µm of polymer, at 2–10 µm L/S; the copper is sputter-seeded and pattern-plated exactly as in bumping.
5. Drop balls, dice the reconstituted wafer.

The tool classes are the bumping line's plus a molder: compression molders from Towa; RDL steppers from Onto Innovation (the former Rudolph JetStep line), Veeco (the former Ultratech) and Canon; sputter systems from Evatec, among others.

> **Worked example WE-L: how much die shift an RDL can tolerate.** The first RDL via must land on the die's pad. Take a ~30 µm pad and a ~15 µm via (representative sizes): the via may miss the pad center by at most (30 − 15) / 2 ≈ **7 µm** before it slides off the pad's edge. Now the shift. Molding drags every die a little toward the wafer center as the compound flows and then shrinks on cure and cool-down, by a fraction ε of its distance r from the center, so δ ≈ ε × r. ε depends on the compound, the carrier and how the compound flowed, and is of order 10⁻⁴ (an estimate): a die at r = 140 mm, near the wafer edge, then moves ~15 µm, twice the budget, while a die near the center barely moves. A single fixed mask therefore cannot serve both, and it gets worse on a 600 mm panel, where r is twice as large. That is why fan-out RDL lithography measures the actual position of every die after molding and either steps the exposure die by die, correcting each field (as a stepper can, since it exposes one field at a time), or generates a custom RDL pattern per package on a maskless writer (Deca Technologies' **adaptive patterning**), and why die shift, not lithography resolution, sets the finest pad pitch a fan-out process can serve.

TSMC's **InFO (Integrated Fan-Out)** made fan-out famous. Introduced in 2016 for the iPhone 7's A10 processor, InFO-PoP replaced the substrate-based flip-chip package-on-package used through the A9 generation (which TSMC and Samsung had dual-sourced). Its innovations: dies are placed face-*up* with tall electroplated copper pillars ("through-InFO vias", TIVs, ~150–200 µm tall) alongside them; after molding, the mold is ground back to expose both the die's copper pads and the TIV tops; RDLs (down to ~2/2 µm L/S, finer than any substrate) are built on top; and the **LPDDR** memory package (low-power DRAM, the phone's main memory) is stacked on the TIVs in a **package-on-package (PoP)** arrangement. The result is thinner than a substrate-based PoP by ~30%, has lower resistance and inductance to the memory, and better thermal performance. Every iPhone **application processor (AP)** since has used an InFO variant (as of 2025), and InFO-on-Substrate (InFO-oS) serves networking and lower-cost multi-die parts. Samsung, ASE, PTI and Innolux pursue panel-level fan-out (**FOPLP**) on 500–600 mm panels to cut cost per area (a 600 mm square panel has ~5× the area of a 300 mm wafer, with less edge waste for rectangular packages), with mixed results as of ~2025. What has gone wrong is everything that scales with size: die shift grows with distance from the panel center (WE-L), a panel that is half silicon and half epoxy warps by more than a wafer and is harder to hold flat for lithography, there is no standard panel size, so every tool is custom and the equipment base is thin, and a single excursion scraps a panel's worth of dies rather than a wafer's. Samsung's panel line packaged the processor of its Galaxy Watch (2018) and remains the best-known production example; as of 2025 FOPLP is spreading for lower-value parts and for large multi-die substrates, while the high-value phone processors stay on InFO wafers.

> **What can go wrong:** **Die shift**: dies move by micrometers to tens of micrometers as the EMC flows and shrinks during molding, so the RDL lithography must measure every die's actual position and adjust each exposure (the same trick LDI plays on substrate panels; WE-L). **Warpage** of a wafer that is half silicon and half epoxy, which fights the lithography's **depth of focus** (the range of heights, only some micrometers for fine lines, over which the projected pattern stays sharp; a wafer that bows more than that cannot be printed in one focus setting) and the bonder's flatness. **RDL cracking** at the die-to-mold step, where the copper crosses from silicon (2.6 ppm/K) onto epoxy (~7–12 ppm/K) and every thermal cycle flexes it. **Mold-to-die delamination**, which lets moisture reach the RDL. **Panel-level yield**: on a 600 mm panel one process excursion scraps many more dies than on a wafer, and the tooling to hold a panel flat to a few µm is still maturing (as of 2025).

## The Package Taxonomy

An engineer chooses a package along four axes. **Pin count**: under ~100 a leadframe suffices; up to ~300 a QFP can still fit leads around the perimeter; beyond that only an area array (BGA) has room. **Power**: a few watts dissipate through a QFN's exposed paddle; hundreds of watts need a flip-chip die with a lid or a bare backside for a cold plate. **Height and footprint**: a phone wants a WLCSP or fan-out part under 1 mm tall and no larger than the die; a server does not care. **Cost per unit**: cents for a leadframe part, dollars to tens of dollars for an FCBGA, thousands for a CoWoS assembly. High-speed signaling pushes toward flip chip regardless of the other axes, because a bond wire's ~1–3 nH cannot carry a multi-GHz signal cleanly.

A package name encodes most of this. "FCBGA-2397, 52.5 × 45 mm, 1.0 mm pitch" says flip chip, ball grid array, 2,397 balls, the body size, and the ball spacing; "QFN-48, 7 × 7 mm, 0.5 mm pitch" says a leadframe part with 48 no-lead pads. The table places the families in history:

| Package | Era | Interconnect | Pin/ball count | Pitch | Typical use today |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DIP (dual in-line package) | 1970s | Wire bond, leadframe | 8–64 | 2.54 mm | Hobbyist, legacy logic |
| SOIC / TSSOP / SOT | 1980s+ | Wire bond, leadframe | 3–56 | 0.5–1.27 mm | Analog, discretes |
| QFP | 1980s+ | Wire bond, leadframe | 32–300 | 0.4–0.8 mm | MCUs, legacy ASICs (application-specific ICs) |
| QFN / DFN | 2000s+ | Wire bond or flip chip, leadframe | 4–100 | 0.4–0.65 mm | PMIC, RF, MCUs, the volume king |
| PGA (pin grid array) | 1980s+ | Wire bond or flip chip, pins into a socket | ~100–1,300+ | 1.27–2.54 mm | Socketed CPUs; now rare (AMD's AM4 was the last mainstream one) |
| PBGA (plastic BGA) | 1990s+ | Wire bond, laminate | 100–1,000 | 0.8–1.27 mm | FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays), networking, mid-range SoCs |
| FCBGA / FCLGA (flip-chip ball / land grid array) | Late 1990s+ | Flip chip, build-up substrate | 500–8,000+ | 0.65–1.0 mm | CPUs, GPUs, high-end SoCs |
| WLCSP | 2000s+ | Direct balls on die (fan-in) | 4–200 | 0.35–0.5 mm | Mobile PMIC, RF, sensors |
| FOWLP (eWLB, InFO) | 2010s+ | RDL over die and mold | 100–1,500 | 0.35–0.5 mm | Smartphone APs, RF, automotive radar |
| 2.5D (CoWoS, EMIB): dies side by side on an interposer or bridge | 2011+ | Microbumps to interposer/bridge on FCBGA | 5,000–10,000+ | 0.65–1.0 mm | AI accelerators, high-performance computing (Module 17) |
| 3D (HBM, SoIC, Foveros): dies stacked vertically | 2015+ | TSVs (through-silicon vias), microbumps or hybrid bonding | Die-to-die 10⁴–10⁶ | 1–40 µm | HBM stacks; stacked SoCs via TSMC SoIC and Intel Foveros, their 3D die-stacking technologies (Modules 15, 17) |

The pattern: as pin counts pass ~300, perimeter leads cannot fit, so the industry moved to area arrays (BGA). As signal speeds and counts passed what a bond wire could serve, it moved to flip chip. As dies passed the reticle limit and as memory bandwidth demanded thousands of wires a few millimeters long, it moved to 2.5D and 3D.

## Package Reliability and Qualification

A package must last 10–20 years in the field but must be qualified in weeks, so every qualification test is an accelerated version of one field stress: hotter, wetter, faster or harder than anything the part will ever see, run for a few hundred hours, and interpreted through an acceleration model that maps test hours to field years. Standards come from **JEDEC**, the industry standards body for semiconductor components, and from the **AEC** (Automotive Electronics Council), whose AEC-Q100 is the car standard. This section covers the package-level stresses and their physics; Module 18 covers the qualification *flows* (JEDEC's JESD47 for commercial parts, AEC-Q100 for automotive) in which these tests are combined with electrical and burn-in tests. The core package tests:

- **Temperature cycling (TC), JESD22-A104.** −40 to +125 °C (condition G) or −55 to +125 °C (condition B), typically 500–1,000 cycles at 1–3 cycles/hour, with electrical test at intervals. Fails: solder fatigue, underfill delamination, die or substrate cracks.
- **HAST (Highly Accelerated Stress Test), JESD22-A110.** 130 °C, 85% **RH** (relative humidity, the fraction of the water vapor the air could hold at that temperature), ~2 atm, 96–264 h with **bias**, a voltage applied during the test so that corrosion and electrochemical migration are driven electrically as in service. It accelerates moisture-driven corrosion, ionic migration and delamination. Unbiased HAST (uHAST, A118) omits the bias; the older THB (temperature-humidity-bias) test (85 °C/85% RH, 1,000 h) tests the same mechanisms more slowly.
- **High-temperature storage (HTS), JESD22-A103.** 150 °C for 1,000 h, driving **intermetallic growth** at wire bonds and bumps: the brittle Au-Al **purple plague** of gold wire on aluminum pads, or Kirkendall voiding at Cu/Sn interfaces (the one-way-diffusion voids defined under Wire Bonding; here copper diffuses into tin faster than tin into copper, and the vacancies it leaves behind coalesce along the interface).
- **Drop test, JESD22-B111.** A board with the packages is dropped to produce a 1,500 g (1,500 times gravity), 0.5 ms half-sine shock, 30 times; it is the pass/fail test for handset packages and the reason low-silver SAC alloys exist.

> **Worked example WE-I: from 1,000 test cycles to years in the field.** A simplified Coffin-Manson acceleration factor for solder fatigue is AF = (ΔT_test / ΔT_field)^n, where ΔT_test and ΔT_field are the temperature swings in the chamber and in service, and n ≈ 1.9 is the fitted exponent for SAC solder. For a −40/+125 °C test (ΔT = 165 K) against a field cycle of 25–85 °C (ΔT = 60 K, a laptop warming up and cooling down once a day): AF = (165/60)^1.9 = 2.75^1.9 ≈ **6.8**. So 1,000 test cycles represent ~6,800 field cycles, about **18 years** at one cycle per day. The honest caveat: the full **Norris-Landzberg** model multiplies this by terms for cycle frequency and for peak temperature. Slow field cycles let the solder **creep** (slow, permanent deformation under a sustained stress, which solder does even at room temperature because 25 °C is already more than half its melting point on the absolute scale, 298 K against 490 K) and so do more damage per cycle than a fast chamber cycle of the same swing, so real qualification uses AF values fitted to the product's mission profile rather than this single exponent.

Before any of these, samples undergo **preconditioning** per J-STD-020 (revision F, 2022): moisture soak to a **Moisture Sensitivity Level (MSL)** followed by three passes through a package-dependent lead-free classification reflow profile, up to 260 °C; the required peak depends on package thickness and volume and is distinct from the actual assembly profile. The MSL system rates how long a package can sit in factory air (30 °C, 60% RH) between opening its dry-pack and being soldered: **MSL 1** = unlimited, **MSL 2** = 1 year, **MSL 2a** = 4 weeks, **MSL 3** = 168 hours (the most common rating for BGAs), MSL 4 = 72 h, MSL 5 = 48 h, MSL 5a = 24 h, MSL 6 = must be baked before use.

> **Intuition:** a popcorn kernel is a sealed shell around a little moisture; heat it and the water flashes to steam at a pressure the shell cannot hold, and it bursts. A molded package that has absorbed moisture is the same kernel: the shell is the epoxy, the weak spot is an internal interface, and the reflow oven is the pan.

The failure it guards against is **popcorning**: epoxy mold compound and substrates absorb ~0.1–0.3 wt% water; at 260 °C, water trapped at an interface (die-to-paddle, mold-to-die, underfill) vaporizes at a pressure of several MPa (the saturated vapor pressure of water at 260 °C is ~4.7 MPa), delaminating the interface and cracking the package with an audible pop. The remedy is baking (125 °C for 24 h) and shipping in dry-packs with desiccant and a humidity indicator card.

> **What can go wrong, and how it is found:** the failure-analysis toolkit is small and universal. **C-SAM** (scanning acoustic microscopy) images internal delaminations and voids non-destructively, because an air gap reflects ultrasound almost totally. **X-ray** shows voids in solder and die attach, wire sweep and bridged balls. **Dye-and-pry** floods a mounted BGA with red dye, pries the package off the board, and any ball that was already cracked shows a red fracture face. **Cross-section**: pot the part in resin, grind and polish to the plane of interest, and look at the joint, the intermetallic thickness and the crack path under a microscope. Environmental chambers for the tests themselves come from ESPEC of Japan and others.

## The Industry: OSATs, Foundry Back Ends, and Equipment

### Why OSATs exist

Packaging is labor- and floor-space-intensive, its tools cost a fraction of a fab's, and its cleanroom class is looser, so chipmakers moved assembly to low-cost regions early (Intel's first offshore assembly plant opened in Penang in 1972) and specialist assemblers grew up alongside them (Anam, the ancestor of Amkor, in Korea in 1968; ASE in Taiwan in 1984). The fabless model completed the split: a company with no fab has no reason to own a packaging plant either, and TSMC's rise created a whole customer base that needed someone to package what the foundry produced. **Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT)** companies package and test chips for fabless firms, foundries and IDMs; they run on volume, thin margins and rapid tool turnover, and cluster in Taiwan, China, Korea and Southeast Asia. **Electronics manufacturing services (EMS)** firms are the next step down the chain, assembling boards; ASE owns one (USI).

### OSATs

The top-10 OSATs had combined 2024 revenue of ~$41.6 billion (TrendForce's May 2025 ranking; this text keeps the 2024 figures because the 2025 ranking was not incorporated at the time of writing). By share of the top-10:

- **ASE Technology Holding** (Taiwan; includes SPIL, acquired 2018, and the USI EMS business): ~$18.5 billion, ~45% of the top-10 and roughly 30% of the entire OSAT market including smaller players. Kaohsiung is the center of gravity.
- **Amkor** (USA, with major plants in Korea, the Philippines, Japan, Taiwan, Vietnam and Portugal): ~$6.3 billion, ~15%.
- **JCET** (China; owns the former STATS ChipPAC of Singapore): ~$5.0 billion, ~12%, growing at double digits.
- **Tongfu Microelectronics** (China; AMD's partner, with the former AMD Suzhou and Penang plants): ~8%; then **Powertech Technology (PTI)** (Taiwan; memory packaging leader), ~5.5%; **Huatian (HT-Tech)** (China), ~5%; and WiseRoad, Hana Micron (Korea), KYEC (Taiwan; test only) and ChipMOS (Taiwan) making up the rest.

### TSMC's Own Back End

TSMC is unusual among foundries in operating a large in-house back end, because it decided in the 2010s that advanced packaging (InFO, CoWoS and **SoIC**, its 3D die-stacking technology, Module 17) was a competitive weapon rather than a commodity. Its **Advanced Packaging (AP)** fabs in Taiwan, as of early 2026:

- **AP1**, Hsinchu: the original site, being repurposed for R&D.
- **AP2**, Tainan: bumping and microbumps, some CoWoS.
- **AP3**, Longtan: InFO, the iPhone AP line.
- **AP5**, Taichung: CoWoS.
- **AP6**, Zhunan: opened June 2023; the main CoWoS and SoIC site.
- **AP7**, Chiayi: under construction to produce from 2026, for CoWoS, SoIC and successors.
- **AP8**, Tainan (Southern Taiwan Science Park): a ~96,000 m² CoWoS complex, ~9× the area of AP6.

TSMC's back-end revenue was ~8–10% of its total in 2024–2025. For its Arizona wafers, TSMC relies on **Amkor's Peoria, Arizona** campus, with TSMC as **anchor tenant** (the committed first customer whose volume justifies the plant) for Apple and NVIDIA parts: Amkor broke ground in October 2025 on a project then sized at ~$7 billion across two phases, signed a 10-year packaging and test services agreement with TSMC in June 2026, and by September 2026 had raised the planned investment to ~$12 billion, with the first phase due to complete in ~2028; TSMC also plans its own packaging on the Arizona campus in a later phase. Intel likewise packages most of its own CPUs (as of 2025) in Malaysia (Penang, Kulim), Vietnam (Ho Chi Minh City, its largest assembly and test site), Chengdu (China), Costa Rica and New Mexico (Rio Rancho, for **Foveros**, Intel's 3D die stacking, Module 17); Samsung packages its memory and logic in Cheonan and Onyang.

### Equipment Vendors

Back-end equipment is a market of order ~$10 billion a year (as of 2025; analyst estimates differ on what to count), a fraction of the front end's ~$100 billion, but concentrated:

| Segment | Leader | Others |
|---|---|---|
| Backgrinding, dicing (blade and stealth) | Disco (Japan), ~70–80% | Accretech/Tokyo Seimitsu, Hamamatsu (stealth laser source) |
| Die attach, flip-chip, TCB, hybrid bonding | Besi (Netherlands), ASMPT (Hong Kong/Singapore) | K&S, Palomar, Shibaura, Fasford |
| HBM TC bonders | Hanmi Semiconductor (Korea, for SK hynix and Micron) | Hanwha Semitech, Semes (Samsung captive), ASMPT |
| Wire bonders | K&S (USA/Singapore), ASMPT | Shinkawa (Yamaha Robotics) |
| Molding | Towa (Japan) in compression; ASMPT, Besi, Yamada in transfer | |
| Temporary bonding/debonding, wafer bonding | EV Group (Austria), SUSS MicroTec (Germany) | TEL |
| Wafer-level plating (bumps, RDL) | Lam Research, Applied Materials | ACM Research, EBARA |
| Substrate laser drilling | Via Mechanics (Japan), Mitsubishi Electric | |
| Substrate LDI | Orbotech (KLA), SCREEN | Via Mechanics |
| Bump and package inspection | Camtek (Israel), Onto Innovation (USA), KLA | Saki, Koh Young |
| Reflow ovens | Heller, BTU (Amtech), Rehm | |

### Cost

For a mainstream chip, assembly and packaging is on the order of 10–20% of the total manufactured chip cost, with test adding a few percent more. A QFN costs cents; a WLCSP a few cents per die; bumping a 300 mm wafer on the order of a few hundred dollars; a mid-range FCBGA several dollars to tens of dollars, most of it the substrate. For an AI accelerator the picture inverts: a CoWoS assembly costs thousands of dollars in packaging and interposer before counting the HBM, so packaging and memory together can exceed 30% of module cost, and the packaging step, not the wafer, sets the volume ceiling. That is the subject of the next module.

## Summary

- A package converts 40–150 µm die terminals into 0.4–1.0 mm board terminals, delivers ~1,000 A at 0.8 V through well under 0.1 mΩ, removes 700+ W, and protects a brittle die for 10–20 years.
- The root problem is CTE mismatch: silicon 2.6 ppm/K versus organic substrate ~15 ppm/K. A 30 mm die's corner bump would shear ~50 µm on cool-down (70% strain); underfill converts that shear into shared bending and buys more than 10× lower strain, roughly 200× more cycles by Coffin-Manson, and 1,000+ survivable thermal cycles.
- FCBGA flow: bump → backgrind → dice → flip-chip join → underfill → lid or mold → mark → ball attach → singulate → test. Leadframe parts branch after dicing into die attach, wire bond, mold, and trim and form.
- Bumping is fab-style lithography plus plating: Ti/Cu UBM, thick resist, a 30–50 µm Cu pillar with a 15–25 µm SnAg cap, at ~0.22 µm/min per A/dm² (about an hour per pillar layer). Cu pillars replaced solder C4 because height no longer depends on pitch and copper resists electromigration.
- Backgrinding takes 775 µm to 300–700 µm (FCBGA), 100–200 µm (wire bond), 30–50 µm (HBM); fine grinding plus stress relief removes the damage layer that would halve die strength; TAIKO rings and temporary carriers handle floppy wafers; Disco has ~70–80% share.
- Dicing: blade (20–50 µm kerf, chipping risk, laser grooving for low-k), stealth (an internal defect plane written at 1,064 nm plus tape expansion, no kerf), plasma (all streets at once, best for tens of thousands of tiny dies).
- Wire bonding still serves ~three-quarters of units: thermosonic copper ball-and-stitch at 15–25 wires/s. A 3 mm wire is ~0.1 Ω and ~3 nH, which is why high-current, high-speed parts moved to flip chip (area-array I/O at ~0.35 mΩ and ~0.05 nH per bump).
- Mass reflow relies on solder self-alignment (±10 µm placement tolerated); TCB holds thin dies flat at ±1–2 µm for fine pitch at 10–30 s per die; underfill choices are CUF, MUF and NCP/NCF.
- The build-up substrate is a miniature PCB: BT core with PTHs, then ABF layers built by SAP (laser microvia, permanganate roughening, electroless seed, LDI, pattern plating); 8–10 µm L/S in volume, 2 µm on the roadmap. Escape routing sets the layer count, and every layer removed is a lamination cycle and a few percent of yield (0.98¹⁸ ≈ 70%).
- Ajinomoto's ABF holds > 90% of the build-up film market; the 2020–2022 shortage was of substrate fabrication capacity (Ibiden, Unimicron, AT&S), not of film; glass cores are the next step for 100 mm-class packages.
- Leadframe + wire bond + transfer mold is the trillion-unit, cents-per-unit world of QFN and QFP; EMC is 70–90% silica in epoxy, molded at 175 °C and 7–10 MPa. Compression molding, a gentle press with no runners, is the variant behind every fan-out wafer and MR-MUF HBM stack, and die shift and warpage are its failure modes.
- A BGA ball supplies ~90% of the board-level joint and sets its height (WE-K); singulation saws strips apart with a thick resin-bond blade, and copper burrs and edge delamination are its defects; finished units ship in trays or tape-and-reel to test and burn-in.
- Moisture absorbed by EMC and substrate flashes to steam at 260 °C reflow (~4.7 MPa), so packages carry MSL ratings (MSL 3 = 168 h floor life) and are baked and dry-packed; 1,000 cycles of −40/+125 °C stand in for ~18 years of daily 60 K cycles (AF ≈ 6.8).
- The TIM between die and lid is the largest thermal resistance in the stack (~17 °C at 700 W for a polymer TIM versus ~3 °C for the silicon); indium solder TIM or a lidless cold plate recovers most of it.
- Fan-out (eWLB, InFO) re-embeds dies in mold so RDL wiring can extend beyond the die edge; InFO-PoP has carried every iPhone processor since the A10. OSATs (ASE ~30%), TSMC's in-house AP fabs, and a concentrated tool base (Disco, Besi, ASMPT, K&S, Towa) make up the industry; packaging is ~10–20% of cost for ordinary chips and > 30% for CoWoS/HBM-class parts.

## Key Numbers

| Quantity | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| CTE of silicon / organic substrate / Cu / SAC305 solder / EMC (below Tg) | 2.6 / ~15 / ~17 / ~22 / ~7–12 ppm/K | The ~12 ppm/K gap between die and substrate drives every strain, warpage and underfill decision |
| Starting 300 mm wafer thickness → after backgrinding | 775 µm → 300–700 µm (FCBGA), 100–200 µm (WLCSP, wire bond), 30–50 µm (HBM DRAM) | Thin dies cool and stack better but warp; below ~100 µm they need TAIKO rings or carriers |
| Coarse / fine grinding wheel grit | #320–#600 / #2000–#8000; damage layer ~10–20 µm → ~1–3 µm | The damage layer halves die strength unless polished off |
| Grind time | ~2 min for 500 µm at 4 µm/s; ~1 min for 30 µm at 0.5 µm/s | A grinder does a wafer in minutes; throughput is set by handling, not grinding |
| TAIKO edge ring width | ~2–3 mm at full thickness | Lets 50–100 µm power wafers be handled without a carrier |
| Blade dicing kerf / spindle speed / feed | 20–50 µm / 30,000–60,000 rpm / 50–150 mm/s | Sets minimum street width and the 5–15 min per wafer |
| Dicing time (WE-D) | ~60 cuts, ~3 min blade time for 10 mm dies on 300 mm; plasma tens of minutes regardless of die count | Plasma wins below few-millimeter dies |
| Stealth dicing laser wavelength | ~1,064 nm (silicon nearly transparent), focused inside the wafer; tape expansion ~10–20% | Zero kerf and no water: the choice for thin memory and image-sensor wafers |
| Cu pillar bump: height / solder cap / pitch | 30–50 µm / 15–25 µm SnAg / 100–130 µm (C4 solder ~130–150 µm; microbumps 36–55 µm) | A pillar decouples stand-off height from pitch |
| UBM stack | Ti (or TiW) ~0.1–0.2 µm + Cu seed ~0.2–0.5 µm | Adhesion, barrier and seed; too thin and repeated reflows consume it |
| Copper plating rate (WE-C) | 0.22 µm/min per A/dm²; ~60 min for a 40 µm pillar at 3 A/dm² | Bumping throughput is set by plating cells, not lithography |
| Solder melting points | SAC305 solidus ~217 °C, liquidus ~220–221 °C; SnAg cap 221–226 °C (by silver content); indium 156.6 °C; Pb-5Sn ~310 °C | Sets reflow profiles and which joint melts when |
| Reflow peak temperature (lead-free) | Production 240–250 °C, 40–90 s above the alloy's liquidus; J-STD-020 classification profile 260 °C | Assembly may intentionally remelt earlier solder joints; the whole package must tolerate its qualified reflow profile |
| Wire bond wire diameter / speed | 15–25 µm / ~15–25 wires per second; ~70–80% of units by count | Still the volume interconnect |
| Wire vs. bump electrical (WE-E) | 3 mm, 25 µm Cu wire: ~0.10 Ω, ~3 nH; Cu pillar 40 µm tall, 50 µm wide: ~0.35 mΩ, ~0.05 nH | Why high-current, high-speed parts are flip chip |
| Per-bump current (WE-F) | ~50 mA per bump for 1,000 A over ~20,000 power/ground bumps; ~2.5 kA/cm² against limits of order ~10⁴ A/cm² (solder) and ~10⁶ A/cm² (copper) | Why the pillar is copper and only the cap is solder |
| Placement accuracy: die attach / flip-chip TCB / hybrid bonding | ±10–25 µm / ±1–2 µm / ±0.1–0.2 µm | Accuracy costs throughput: 20,000 to hundreds of units per hour |
| Die-attach bond-line resistance, 5 × 5 mm die (WE-J) | Silver epoxy 25 µm: ~0.33 K/W; solder 50 µm: ~0.04 K/W; sintered Ag 30 µm: ~0.006 K/W | Epoxy is fine at 10 W, not at 100 W; a void's damage is local, not average |
| Corner-bump CTE displacement, 30 mm die, ΔT 192 K (WE-A) | ~50 µm (γ ≈ 70% without underfill) | Underfill cuts strain > 10×, worth ~200× in cycles |
| Thermal stack at 700 W over 8.1 cm² (WE-B) | 500 µm Si ~2.9 °C; 100 µm polymer TIM ~17 °C; 100 µm indium ~1.1 °C | The TIM is the hottest layer; STIM or a lidless cold plate saves ~15 °C |
| ABF film thickness / laser microvia diameter / SAP line-space | 25–40 µm / 30–70 µm / ~8–10 µm in volume, 5 µm leading, 2 µm roadmap | L/S sets the layer count through escape routing |
| Escape routing (traces per channel at 150 µm pitch) | ~3 at 10/10 µm; ~20 at 2/2 µm | 3–4 signal layers versus one |
| Substrate yield compounding (WE-H) | 0.98¹⁸ ≈ 70%; 0.98¹² ≈ 78% | Every removed layer is worth a few percent of yield |
| ABF market share held by Ajinomoto | > 90% (as of 2025) | A highly concentrated supply of build-up dielectric for high-performance substrates; not every FCBGA uses ABF |
| Large AI GPU substrate | ~80–100+ mm side, 20+ layers, ~1 mm core; 4,000–7,000 BGA balls at 1.0 mm pitch | Only a few dozen good units per 510 × 515 mm panel |
| EMC composition / transfer mold conditions | 70–90 wt% silica; 175 °C, 7–10 MPa, 60–120 s, PMC 175 °C 4–6 h | Silica sets CTE; the pressure is why wires sweep |
| Compression molding | ~120–175 °C, pressure of order ~1–5 MPa (estimate), under vacuum, minutes in the mold; no runners or gates | The molding process behind every fan-out wafer and MR-MUF HBM stack |
| BGA ball vs. board paste (WE-K) | 0.6 mm ball ≈ 0.113 mm³; board paste deposit ≈ 0.012 mm³ of metal; ball ≈ 90% of the joint | The ball sets joint height; a ~450 µm joint sees ~5% strain where a 60 µm one would see ~35% |
| Package saw | Resin-bond blade of order ~0.2–0.3 mm thick, kerf ~0.2–0.3 mm, streets ~0.3 mm (estimates) | Copper burrs and edge delamination are the singulation defects |
| Fan-out die-shift budget (WE-L) | ~7 µm allowed for a 15 µm via on a 30 µm pad; shift ≈ ε × r, ~15 µm at the wafer edge for ε ~10⁻⁴ | Why RDL lithography measures every die and adjusts each exposure |
| MSL 3 floor life / bake / popcorn vapor pressure at 260 °C | 168 h at ≤30 °C/60% RH / bake depends on package and exposure / ~4.7 MPa | Why BGAs ship in dry-packs |
| Temperature cycling / HAST conditions | −40 to +125 °C, 500–1,000 cycles / 130 °C, 85% RH, 96–264 h | The two tests that catch fatigue and moisture failures |
| Thermal-cycling acceleration (WE-I) | AF = (165/60)^1.9 ≈ 6.8; 1,000 cycles ≈ 18 years of daily 60 K cycles in this simplified fatigue model | How weeks of testing stand in for years of life |
| Top-10 OSAT revenue 2024 / ASE share of top-10 | ~$41.6 B / ~45% (~30% of the whole OSAT market) | One company packages a third of the world's outsourced chips |
| Packaging + test share of chip cost | ~10–20% typical; > 30% for CoWoS/HBM-class parts | For some AI ramps, qualified packaging capacity has limited output; cost shares alone do not identify the bottleneck |

## Key Players

The company's home country is not the full factory map: JCET, for example, reported manufacturing locations in China, Korea and Singapore. Its packaging and test business serves international customers. This is why supplier concentration should be assessed by the actual plant, process and qualified capacity, not by assigning every package to a corporate flag. ## Common Misconceptions

- **"Packaging is a low-tech afterthought."** → A leading FCBGA substrate is a 20-layer laminate with 8 µm copper lines, laser vias, and micrometer-level registration across a half-meter panel; bumping uses fab lithography and plating; TCB places dies to ±1 µm. Packaging now sets the volume and cost ceiling for AI accelerators.
- **"Wire bonding is obsolete."** → It is obsolete for high-pin-count, high-speed parts, but by unit count roughly three-quarters of all packaged devices are still wire-bonded, on copper wire, at 15–25 wires per second.
- **"Underfill is just glue to hold the chip on."** → Underfill is the structural element that converts an unsurvivable ~50 µm shear displacement at the die corners into a shared bending of die and substrate. Without it, flip chip on organic substrates would fail in a few thermal cycles.
- **"Thinner dies are always better."** → Thin dies conduct heat better and stack more, but they warp, are hard to handle below ~100 µm without carriers or TAIKO rings, and lose fracture strength unless the grinding damage layer is polished off. Large FCBGA dies are deliberately kept at 300–700 µm.
- **"A shortage of ABF means Ajinomoto is out of stock."** → The 2020–2022 "ABF shortage" was mainly a shortage of ABF *substrate* fabrication capacity at Ibiden, Unimicron, and peers (two-year plant build cycles), with the film itself a secondary constraint. Ajinomoto sells to substrate makers, not chip companies.
- **"Stealth dicing is just a laser saw."** → A laser saw ablates material from the surface; stealth dicing writes a plane of defects *inside* the silicon with a beam the surface barely absorbs, and the wafer is then cleaved by stretching the tape. There is no kerf and no debris.
- **"The die is always the most expensive part of a package."** → For many mid-range FCBGAs the substrate costs more than the whole assembly process and can rival the die; for a large GPU the substrate alone is $100–300, and a CoWoS assembly's packaging and HBM exceed 30% of module cost.
- **"Lead-free solder was a drop-in replacement for tin-lead."** → SAC melts at ~217 °C against ~183 °C for eutectic tin-lead, ~35 °C higher. That pushed reflow peaks to 240–250 °C in production and 260 °C in qualification, which is what made moisture sensitivity and popcorning a first-order problem, created the MSL system, and forced the reformulation of mold compounds, laminates and underfills to survive the hotter reflow.

## Where This Fits in the Supply Chain

Module 15 ended with finished, probed memory wafers, and Module 14 with logic wafers whose dies carry a wafer-sort map of known-good positions. This module consumes those wafers plus a second stream of inputs that never touch a fab: ABF film from Ajinomoto, BT cores from Mitsubishi Gas Chemical, build-up substrates from Ibiden and Unimicron, leadframes from Mitsui High-tec, mold compound from Sumitomo Bakelite, tapes from Nitto Denko, solder spheres, wire, and TIMs, all processed on tools from Disco, Besi, ASMPT, K&S, and Towa. Its outputs are singulated, marked, ball-attached packages: QFNs and QFPs by the billions from ASE and JCET, FCBGAs from Amkor and ASE, and InFO packages from TSMC's Longtan fab, shipped in trays to final test (Module 18). Module 17 takes the same bumping, substrate, TCB, and molding building blocks and adds silicon interposers, TSVs, and hybrid bonding to build CoWoS and SoIC, the packages that carry NVIDIA's GPUs and their HBM stacks; those, after test, become the SXM modules (NVIDIA's GPU module form factor) and NVL72 racks (72 GPUs in one liquid-cooled cabinet) of Module 19.

# Module 17: Advanced Packaging: CoWoS, SoIC and Chiplets

A large GPU needs more than a powerful compute die: it needs a way to connect that die to nearby memory. Pick up an NVIDIA Blackwell **GPU** package (a graphics processing unit, the chip that does the arithmetic of AI training; the B200 is the Blackwell data-centre part) and you are holding five kinds of object glued into one. On top, under a copper lid, sit two ~800 mm² logic **dies** (a die is one rectangular chip cut from a 300 mm wafer) and eight stacks of **high bandwidth memory (HBM)**, the memory that feeds the GPU. Under them lies a slab of silicon carrying wiring but no transistors, the **interposer**. Under that is a 20-layer **organic** laminate (a polymer-and-glass-fibre board, the green material of a circuit board, as opposed to silicon), and under that a grid of solder balls.

The assembly exists because chip-making ran into three walls at once. A lithography scanner cannot print a die larger than 26 × 33 mm, so the biggest GPU must be two dies. Defects fall on a wafer at random, so the fraction of dies that survive falls exponentially with area. And each HBM stack needs ~1,600 signal wires entering the GPU through ~12 mm of its edge, which no organic board can route: its wires are ~10 µm wide and its **vias** (plated holes that join one wiring layer to the next) ~50 µm across, while HBM's contacts sit only 55 µm apart. Joining several chips on a wire-only silicon slab and then on a laminate is TSMC's **CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate)**, the subject of this module.

It is hard because the assembly is unforgiving. The parts alone (two GPU dies, eight HBM stacks, interposer, substrate) are worth ~$5,000–7,000 before assembly, and once the solder joints are made and locked in epoxy there is no taking them apart: one open solder joint among the ~250,000 microbumps under the dies and the tens of thousands of larger bumps under the interposer (the Anatomy section counts them) scraps the lot. The stack is a sandwich of materials that expand at different rates, so every trip through a ~245 °C solder oven bends it by hundreds of micrometres, enough to lift corner joints off their pads. And it is capacity-bound: from 2023 through 2026 the number of these assemblies TSMC could build each month, not the number of transistors it could print, set the ceiling on how many AI accelerators existed.

By the end of this module you will be able to draw the cross-section from lid to solder ball with the thickness of each layer; walk the six-step flow from bare interposer wafer to tested package and say why each step comes in the order it does; explain why the CoWoS-L variant exists and what nearly went wrong with it on Blackwell; explain what hybrid bonding does that solder cannot; and convert a headline "wafers per month" figure into GPUs.

## Before you start

- **Die, wafer and yield (Module 13).** A die is one rectangular chip cut from a 300 mm wafer that holds tens to hundreds of them; defects land at random, so bigger dies fail more often and yield (the fraction of good dies) falls exponentially with area.
- **The lithography field and the reticle (Module 07).** A scanner images a 152 mm square quartz **reticle** (the photomask) onto the wafer at 4× reduction; the largest rectangle it prints in one shot is 26 × 33 mm.
- **Copper damascene wiring and CMP (Module 12).** Chip wiring is made by etching trenches into an insulator, filling them with plated copper and polishing flat by **chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP)**; all wiring in this module, including the interposer's, is built this way.
- **Plasma etch and the Bosch process (Module 09).** A plasma removes material where a mask leaves it exposed; the Bosch process makes deep, straight-walled holes in silicon by alternating short etch and wall-protection cycles.
- **Thin films: CVD, PVD, ALD (Module 06).** Chemical vapour deposition (gases react on the surface to leave a film), sputtering (atoms knocked off a target land on the wafer) and atomic layer deposition (one atomic layer per gas pulse) lay down films from nanometres to micrometres thick.
- **HBM (Module 15).** High bandwidth memory is 8–16 DRAM dies (dynamic random-access memory, the working memory of every computer) stacked on a base die with a 1,024-bit interface, sold as tested stacks with solder bumps on a 55 µm grid underneath.
- **Flip-chip, bumps, underfill, ABF substrate and CTE (Module 16).** A die is mounted face-down on solder bumps onto a laminate built from Ajinomoto build-up film (ABF); materials grow at different rates per degree (the coefficient of thermal expansion, CTE, quoted in ppm/°C, parts per million per degree, i.e. micrometres of growth per metre per degree: silicon 2.6 ppm/°C, laminate ~15), and underfill, an epoxy glue between die and substrate, makes the two bend together so the joints do not shear.
- **Capacitance and energy per bit (school physics).** A wire and its surroundings form a capacitor; sending a bit means charging it to the supply voltage, costing energy of order C·V² per transition, so longer wires cost more per bit.
- **Thermal conductivity and thermal resistance (school physics).** Thermal conductivity (W/m·K) says how easily heat flows through a material; thermal resistance (K/W) says how many degrees of rise each watt causes across a part. They are the heat analogues of conductance and resistance.


**How to read the numerical examples.** Public product specifications and dated company statements are attributed where checked. Unattributed geometry, recipe, yield, throughput and price ranges are representative teaching assumptions or reported estimates, not disclosed production data. They illustrate a mechanism or a calculation; applying them to a named chip requires its process, configuration, date and measurement definition. The accompanying review identifies remaining evidence gaps.

## Why the Package Became the Chip

> **Intuition: three walls.** Think of the three constraints as a print size you cannot exceed, a coin toss you lose more often the bigger the die, and a highway with 1,600 lanes that has to enter a 12 mm gate. The first is the reticle: the scanner's projector has one frame size, and a conventional single-field die must fit the frame; specialized wafer-scale designs use stitching across fields. The second is yield: every square millimetre is another toss of a slightly loaded coin, and the die survives only if every toss comes up heads, so doubling the area squares the odds of survival. The third is HBM: a memory stack talks over ~1,600 signal wires spaced 55 µm apart, and all of them must land on a die edge about 12 mm long. No one of these forced the industry to build packages out of several chips; all three together did.

### The reticle wall

A scanner exposes a rectangular **field** by sweeping a slit of light across the reticle while the wafer stage moves in synchrony (Module 07). The reticle is a 152 mm (6 inch) square quartz plate carrying the pattern at 4× its final size. Only a ~104 × 132 mm patch of it can be imaged without distortion, and 104/4 × 132/4 = 26 × 33 mm on the wafer. That 858 mm² is the **reticle limit**, the largest die that can be printed in one exposure, and it has not moved since the 1990s. NVIDIA's GH100 (the die inside the H100, the 2022 generation before Blackwell) is 814 mm², each Blackwell die is ~800 mm², and every large data-centre part since Volta (NVIDIA's 2017 data-centre GPU generation) has sat within a few percent of this ceiling.

High-NA **EUV** (extreme ultraviolet lithography, the 13.5 nm-wavelength scanners of Module 08) makes it worse. **Numerical aperture (NA)** is how wide a cone of light the lens gathers, and a wider cone resolves finer detail; ASML's EXE:5000 is the first EUV scanner at NA 0.55 rather than 0.33. Its optics are **anamorphic**, reducing 4× in one direction and 8× in the other, so the printed field is half as tall: 26 × 16.5 mm = 429 mm². Dies larger than that on High-NA layers require **reticle stitching**, two half-field exposures whose edges overlap by a few micrometres with matched **critical dimensions (CD)**, the widths of the smallest printed features. The reticle wall is a physical fact and the first reason logic must be split into pieces.

### The yield math of big dies

The second reason is statistical. A larger die gives a defect more area to hit. In the simple model used here, defects land independently like raindrops, at an average **defect density D0** per unit area, and any counted defect makes the die fail. This is a model for the calculation, not a claim that every physical imperfection destroys a real chip.

Let A be die area and Y the fraction of dies that survive. A·D0 is the average number of counted defects per die. The **Poisson model** gives Y = exp(−A·D0), the probability of receiving none; exp(x) means e raised to the power x. As the expected defect count rises, the surviving fraction falls. Units matter: D0 is quoted per cm², so an 800 mm² die is A = 8 cm², and at a mature-node D0 of ~0.1/cm², A·D0 = 8 × 0.1 = 0.8. Then an 800 mm² die yields exp(−0.8) ≈ 45%, a 400 mm² die exp(−0.4) ≈ 67%, and a 1,600 mm² die exp(−1.6) ≈ 20%. Splitting a design in two raises the good silicon fraction per wafer from ~45% to ~67% because each half is judged independently (Module 13 covers the models). The practical gain comes from testing and selecting the pieces before joining them: a defective half no longer forces an otherwise good neighboring half to be discarded with it. The eventual package still needs all of its selected pieces and their connections to work. The corollary is that a **chiplet** strategy (building one product from several smaller dies; the Chiplet section) only pays if the connections between the pieces cost almost nothing in power, latency and area relative to on-die wires.

### HBM's thousands of wires

**High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)** (Module 15) is a stack of 8–16 DRAM dies over a base die, and its defining feature is the width of its interface: 1,024 data bits for HBM2 through HBM3E, 2,048 for HBM4. Each bit toggles at 6.4–9.6 Gb/s in HBM3E, and the interface is meant to consume a few picojoules per bit. A **picojoule (pJ)** is 10⁻¹² J, and the scale to remember is that a link moving 8 TB/s (6.4 × 10¹³ bits per second) at 1 pJ per bit burns 64 W.

Why does the wire's length affect energy? A wire has capacitance to surrounding conductors: moving its voltage requires moving charge. Sending a 1 after a 0 means charging that capacitance C to the supply voltage V, which draws energy of order C·V² from the supply per transition. C measures how much charge the wiring stores per volt; V is the voltage swing in this simplified picture. The useful lesson is that more capacitance costs more energy each time the signal changes, even if the wire's resistance is small. Capacitance grows with length: a trace on a circuit board carries ~0.1–0.2 pF per millimetre (1 pF = 10⁻¹² F), so a 10 cm board trace is ~10–20 pF, while a few millimetres of fine interposer wire is only tens to a few hundred femtofarads (1 fF = 10⁻¹⁵ F), one to two orders of magnitude less. Energy per bit therefore tracks wire length, and HBM's few-pJ target is only reachable if the wires are short (a few millimetres), thin and numerous.

Numerous means the count of **I/Os** (input/output pins, one wire's connection point on the die). One HBM3E stack has on the order of 1,500–1,800 signal I/Os once clocks, **command/address** lines (the wires that tell the memory which row and column to read), **strobes** (timing wires that tell the receiver when to sample the data wires) and parity are counted, and ~5,000–6,000 **microbumps** (the ~25 µm solder-capped copper posts that connect a die to whatever is beneath it; fully described in the Anatomy section) including power and ground. An HBM stack is ~11–12 mm wide and butts against the GPU edge, so each stack's ~1,600 signals must enter the GPU through ~12 mm of edge, and the GPU's receiving circuits sit within ~10 mm of that edge. Eight stacks need ~13,000 signal lines.

Now the density arithmetic. Wiring is quoted as **line/space**: the width of a wire and the gap to its neighbour. The **pitch**, the centre-to-centre spacing, is their sum. An organic build-up substrate (Module 16) routes copper at ~8–15 µm line/space with ~50–60 µm microvias; at 10/10 µm the pitch is 20 µm, so a layer holds 1,000/20 = 50 wires per millimetre at best. A silicon interposer patterned with the copper damascene process of Module 12 on a **65 nm-class** process (a chip-making generation from ~2006, named for its smallest printed feature; its tools are old, paid-off and cheap, as the CoWoS-S section explains) routes at ~0.4–2 µm line/space; at 0.4/0.4 µm the pitch is 0.8 µm and one layer holds 1,000/0.8 = 1,250 wires per millimetre. That is a ~25× gap at the finest lines, 20–50× across the useful range, and it is the mechanism behind "HBM requires **2.5D**," the industry's term for dies placed side by side on an interposer. There is a second, blunter reason: even with enough layers, HBM's 55 µm-pitch microbumps cannot land on an organic substrate at all, because its smallest via is ~50 µm and the pad around a via is ~65 µm (Module 16); there is no room for a bump every 55 µm.

### Bandwidth per millimetre of shoreline, picojoules per bit

Two figures of merit organize the field. **Bandwidth density** is quoted as GB/s per millimetre of die edge (the **shoreline**, since side-by-side dies connect only along the edges that face each other) for side-by-side links, or per mm² of face for dies stacked on top of each other. **Energy per bit** is in pJ/bit. 2.5D, again, means dies side by side on an interposer or bridge; **3D** means dies stacked face to face.

A key to the table's rows: **BEOL** (back end of line) is the copper wiring built on top of the transistors inside a chip. **SoIC** and **Foveros Direct** are TSMC's and Intel's names for **hybrid bonding**, fusing two dies' copper pads directly with no solder (the SoIC section). **EMIB** is Intel's version of a small silicon bridge under two die edges (the Competitors section). **UCIe** is the open industry standard for chip-to-chip links inside a package (the Chiplet section); it comes in two tiers, an **advanced-package** version for interposers and bridges and a **standard-package** version for organic substrates, which is why it appears in two rows below (the Chiplet section gives their numbers). **C4** bumps (controlled collapse chip connection) are the ~100 µm solder bumps under an interposer or die, **RDL** (redistribution layer) is the interposer's own wiring, layers whose only job is to re-route connections from one pattern of contact points to another (the Anatomy section), and **ABF** is the epoxy film an organic substrate's layers are made of (Module 16). **Infinity Fabric (IF)** is AMD's on-package link. A **SerDes** (serializer/deserializer) is a circuit that packs many bits onto one very fast wire and unpacks them at the far end, used whenever wires are scarce, as on a board or in a cable; **NVLink** is NVIDIA's GPU-to-GPU SerDes link and **PCIe** the standard board-level one. An **800G transceiver** is a pluggable optical module carrying 800 Gb/s, and **COUPE** is TSMC's optical engine that sits on the package instead (the Two Handoffs section). Approximate values as of ~2025:

| Link type | Physical medium | Bump/pad pitch | Bandwidth density (edge) | Energy per bit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-die wire | BEOL Cu | n/a | Effectively unlimited | ~0.01–0.1 pJ/bit |
| Hybrid-bonded 3D (SoIC, Foveros Direct) | Cu-Cu direct | 6–9 µm | Areal: >1 TB/s per mm² | ~0.05–0.2 pJ/bit |
| 2.5D on Si interposer or bridge (CoWoS, EMIB; UCIe advanced) | Cu pillar µbump on Si RDL | 25–55 µm | ~0.5–1.3 TB/s/mm | ~0.25–0.6 pJ/bit |
| HBM3E interface (2.5D) | µbumps on interposer | ~50–55 µm | ~100 GB/s per mm of stack edge | ~2.5–4 pJ/bit incl. DRAM I/O |
| Organic substrate die-to-die (UCIe standard, AMD Ryzen IF) | C4 bumps on ABF | 100–130 µm | ~30–200 GB/s/mm | ~0.5–2 pJ/bit |
| Board-level SerDes (NVLink, PCIe 5/6) | PCB traces, connectors | n/a | ~10–50 GB/s/mm | ~5–10 pJ/bit |
| Pluggable optics (800G transceiver) | Fibre | n/a | Limited by how many plug sockets fit on the switch's front panel | ~15–30 pJ/bit |
| Co-packaged optics on CoWoS (COUPE) | Fibre to package edge | n/a | ~1.6 Tb/s per engine | ~5 pJ/bit or lower (target) |

Every step a signal takes off the package costs roughly 10× in energy per bit. The reason is the one above, plus one more: longer wires mean more capacitance to charge, and once a wire is long enough to distort the signal (a board trace at tens of Gb/s), each end needs SerDes circuits that equalize and re-time it, and those circuits burn far more than the wire itself. Packaging technology exists to keep the fattest data flows on the top rows of the table.

> **Worked example: the HBM power budget, and why GDDR could not do it.** A B200 has eight HBM3E stacks delivering ~8 TB/s, i.e. 6.4 × 10¹³ bits per second. At a realistic ~3 pJ/bit for the HBM3E interface (DRAM I/O plus the **PHY**, the transmit and receive circuits that drive and sense the wires, over a few mm of interposer wire), running flat out costs 6.4 × 10¹³ × 3 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 190 W, a large but survivable slice of a 1,000 W package, and real workloads rarely sustain peak bandwidth. **GDDR** is the graphics memory soldered around a gaming GPU on the circuit board; delivering the same 8 TB/s from GDDR-class memory over an organic package and board at ~7 pJ/bit would be ~450 W for memory traffic alone, before the impossibility of fitting the hundreds of 20+ Gb/s pins along the die edge. HBM4 pushes the other way: it doubles the width to 2,048 bits and holds per-pin speed near 8 Gb/s, giving ~2 TB/s per stack at lower energy per bit, at the cost of ~2× the signal I/Os and a base die built on a logic process rather than a DRAM one. More wires, shorter and slower, is the consistent direction.

## Anatomy of a CoWoS Package, Top to Bottom

Before the history and the variants, here is the object itself, as a vertical section through a Blackwell-class part, from the cooler down to the circuit board. Every later section refers back to one of these layers.

1. **Lid.** A ~2–3 mm nickel-plated copper plate covering the whole package top. It spreads heat from the dies to the cooler, protects them, and gives the cold plate (the water-cooled copper block of Module 19) a flat face to press on.
2. **TIM1.** A **thermal interface material** is a soft heat conductor that fills the microscopic air gaps between two solid faces; TIM1 is the layer between the die backs and the lid (TIM2 is between lid and cooler). Indium solder, a filled polymer or a liquid-metal alloy, 50–100 µm thick.
3. **Dies.** Two GPU dies of ~0.7 mm-thick silicon, face-down, and eight HBM stacks (8–16 thinned DRAM dies on a base die) of nearly the same total height, so that one flat lid can touch all of them. The gaps between them are filled with **mold compound**, an epoxy loaded with silica powder that is pressed around the dies and hardens into a rigid slab, ground back so the die backs are exposed.
4. **Microbumps.** Each die's face carries copper pillars ~20–30 µm tall and ~25 µm across, capped with ~10–15 µm of tin-silver solder, on a 40–55 µm grid; after joining, the die stands ~25–35 µm above the interposer. **Pitch** is the centre-to-centre spacing of neighbouring bumps, and it sets the count: at 45 µm pitch one square millimetre holds (1,000/45)² ≈ 490 bumps, so an ~800 mm² die can carry ~100,000 of them.
5. **Interposer.** A ~100 µm-thick slab of silicon, 48 × 58 mm on Blackwell. On its top face are four or five layers of copper RDL wiring (the redistribution layers defined above: wiring whose only job is to re-route connections from one pattern of contact points to another) at 0.4–2 µm line/space. Through it run **through-silicon vias (TSVs)**, copper-filled holes ~10 µm across and ~100 µm deep, one per connection that has to cross the slab. On its bottom face a single coarse RDL layer spreads the TSVs out to **C4 pads**, the landing pads for the next layer of solder.
6. **C4 bumps.** Solder bumps ~80–100 µm in diameter on a 130–180 µm pitch, tens of thousands of them, joining the interposer's bottom to the substrate.
7. **Substrate.** An organic **build-up laminate** 2–3 mm thick and 80–100 mm on a side: a ~1 mm rigid **core** of glass-fibre cloth in epoxy, with 10–12 **build-up layers** on each side, each a ~30 µm sheet of **ABF (Ajinomoto build-up film)** epoxy carrying ~10 µm copper lines and laser-drilled vias (Module 16). Its expansion rate is the number that dominates the rest of this module. **CTE** is the coefficient of thermal expansion, the fractional growth per degree; 2.6 ppm/°C means 2.6 µm of growth per metre per degree. The values below recur throughout.
8. **BGA balls.** A **ball grid array**: several thousand solder balls of SAC305 (tin with 3% silver and 0.5% copper, the standard lead-free solder) ~0.6 mm in diameter on a ~1 mm pitch, joining the substrate to the board.
9. **Board.** The GPU module's printed circuit board (the SXM module of Module 19, NVIDIA's GPU module form factor), whose millimetre-scale features the package has now stepped down to.

| Material | Where it sits in the stack | CTE (ppm/°C) |
|---|---|---|
| Silicon | Dies, interposer, bridge chiplets (CoWoS-L) | 2.6 |
| Copper | Wiring, pillars, TSVs, lid | ~17 |
| SnAg / SAC solder | Microbumps, C4, BGA | ~22 |
| Epoxy mold compound | Around the dies and, in CoWoS-L, the interposer | ~8–12 below its glass transition (the softening temperature, ~150–200 °C), more above |
| ABF build-up layers (in-plane) | Substrate wiring layers | ~15–20 |
| Glass-epoxy core | Substrate core | ~10–15 |
| Polyimide RDL | CoWoS-R and CoWoS-L interposers | ~20–50 |
| Organic substrate as a whole (in-plane) | Substrate | ~10–17 |

> **Intuition: the scale of the thing.** The interposer is as thick as a sheet of printer paper (~100 µm) and a little smaller than a playing card, and it carries wiring so fine that 175 of its 0.4 µm lines would fit across one human hair (~70 µm). The microbumps sit about as close together as the pixels on a phone screen. The two GPU dies dissipate ~1,000 W over ~16 cm², the area of a large postage stamp, which is ~10× the heat flux of a kitchen hotplate. Everything about CoWoS follows from those three facts: paper-thin silicon that must be handled, wires that must line up to a fraction of a micrometre, and heat that must leave through a lid.

> **Why it matters downstream.** Every layer in the list above is a thermal resistance in series: heat from the transistors crosses ~0.7 mm of silicon, 50–100 µm of TIM1, ~2–3 mm of copper lid, then TIM2 and the cold plate. Module 19 adds these up to a junction-to-coolant resistance (the junction is the transistor layer, the hottest point) of ~0.05–0.1 K/W, and the thickness of each layer chosen here, especially the TIM1 bond line, is a term in that sum.

## CoWoS: A Short History

TSMC's first 2.5D product was not a GPU. In 2011 Xilinx shipped the Virtex-7 2000T, four 28 nm **FPGA** dies (an FPGA is a chip whose logic is wired up after manufacture by loading a configuration) side by side on a passive 65 nm silicon interposer with more than 10,000 die-to-die connections. Xilinx called it Stacked Silicon Interconnect; TSMC generalized the process and in 2012 named it CoWoS. The interposer started as a 775 µm wafer and was thinned to ~100 µm to reveal its TSVs; the flow, chip-on-wafer first and then wafer-on-substrate, is the one used for a Blackwell today.

The GPU era began with HBM. AMD's Fiji (Radeon Fury X, 2015) was the first GPU with HBM, but its interposer came from **UMC** (Taiwan's second foundry) and assembly from **ASE** (the world's largest outsourced assembly house). NVIDIA's Tesla P100 (2016) put a 610 mm² GP100 die and four HBM2 stacks on CoWoS, and every NVIDIA data-centre GPU since (V100, A100, H100, B200 and Rubin, the generation after Blackwell) has used it, as have Google's **TPUs** (its tensor processing units, the in-house AI chips), AMD's MI250/MI300, Broadcom's and Marvell's custom AI **ASICs** (application-specific integrated circuits, chips designed for one customer's workload), and Amazon's Trainium (its in-house training accelerator). That is how one company's back-end capacity became the industry's bottleneck.

## The Three CoWoS Variants

The problem all three variants solve is the same: connect dies with wiring ~25× denser than a laminate can hold, over an area 3–10× larger than any single lithography exposure, and keep the whole sandwich flat and electrically sound through several trips to 245 °C. They differ in what the interposer is made of.

> **Intuition: three breadboards.** CoWoS-S is a breadboard carved from silicon: every wire on it is as fine as chip wiring, everywhere, whether it needs to be or not. CoWoS-R is a plastic breadboard, cheap and flexible, with wires five times coarser. CoWoS-L is the plastic breadboard with small silicon patches glued in only where the fine wires must be, under the seams where a GPU meets an HBM stack or another GPU. Each step trades cost and mechanical fit against uniformity.

### CoWoS-S: the silicon interposer

**CoWoS-S** (S for silicon) uses a full-size passive silicon interposer, made on a 300 mm wafer on **depreciated** 65 nm-class tools: machines bought around 2006 and long since paid off, so an interposer wafer costs a fraction of a logic wafer. It has four or five RDL layers at 0.4–2 µm line/space, microbump pads on top, and TSVs of ~10 µm diameter and ~100 µm depth connecting the front wiring to backside C4 pads. It contains no transistors, but it can contain **deep-trench capacitors** (TSMC's iCAP option, hundreds of nF per mm²): capacitors made by etching narrow trenches into the silicon and lining them with dielectric and electrode, which pack a large capacitance into a small footprint. Their job is **decoupling**. When millions of transistors switch in the same nanosecond the die draws a current spike that the substrate's wires cannot deliver in time, so the supply voltage sags; a capacitor sitting 100 µm below the die is a local charge reservoir that fills the gap. The arithmetic is Q = C·ΔV, the charge a capacitor gives up equals its capacitance times the voltage drop you are willing to allow: hundreds of nF per mm² means a few µF under a GPU, and a few µF × a tolerable ~50 mV of sag ≈ 0.1–0.2 µC of charge, which at 100 A (t = Q/I) lasts ~1–2 ns. That is exactly the timescale the substrate cannot cover. Its supply wires are millimetres long, and a long wire has **inductance**, the property of a conductor that opposes any change in the current through it (as mass opposes a change in speed), so the current from the substrate cannot ramp up in a nanosecond; it takes over on a timescale of ~tens of nanoseconds, by which time the interposer's capacitors must have carried the spike. This is an underappreciated advantage of silicon over organic.

The interposer is much bigger than a reticle, and its size is quoted as a **reticle multiple**, the interposer area divided by 858 mm². H100's is ~2.5× (~2,100–2,200 mm²); the 2024–2026 generation is 3.3× (~2,800 mm²); TSMC has qualified 5.5× (~4,700 mm², 12 HBM stacks) and roadmapped 9.5× (~8,000 mm² on a 120 × 150 mm substrate) for 2027. The lithography tool here is a **stepper**, the older, simpler cousin of the scanner: it exposes one whole field at a time from a stationary reticle instead of sweeping a slit across it, with the same 26 × 33 mm field, and the interposer's 0.4 µm wiring needs nothing better. Since the stepper exposes 858 mm² at a time, every RDL layer is patterned with multiple **stitched** exposures: the layout is split into fields, each exposed separately, with wires crossing a boundary drawn with overlap. **Overlay** is how precisely one exposure lines up with another, in nanometres, and here it is unforgiving: a 0.4 µm wire that crosses a stitch boundary offset by a quarter of its width loses a quarter of its cross-section, raising its resistance and risking an open, so stitching 0.4 µm lines demands overlay well under 100 nm.

The drawbacks scale with size. A 2,800 mm² interposer means ~16 per wafer, and one killer defect in the RDL or a TSV scraps the whole piece. Silicon (CTE 2.6 ppm/°C) is also a poor thermal-expansion match to the organic substrate below (~10–17 ppm/°C), manageable at H100 scale and increasingly not beyond.

### CoWoS-R: the organic RDL interposer

**CoWoS-R** (R for RDL) replaces the silicon with an organic RDL interposer built with TSMC's **InFO** fan-out process, in which dies are embedded in epoxy and wiring is built on top of them (the Fan-Out section describes it fully). The dielectric is **polyimide**, a heat-resistant polymer film (the orange material of flexible cables), with copper at ~2 µm line/space in several (up to ~6) RDL layers, no TSVs and no TIVs: each layer's vias (~5–10 µm holes opened in the polyimide) drop straight down through the stack to the C4 pads, so the whole interposer is a thin stack of polymer and copper built layer by layer on a carrier and released from it, exactly as the Fan-Out section describes. It is cheaper and better CTE-matched to the substrate. It also has lower line capacitance, because polyimide's **dielectric constant** (the factor by which a material filling the gap between two conductors multiplies their capacitance, relative to empty space) is ~3 against ~4 for silicon dioxide and there is no conductive silicon beneath the wires to act as the capacitor's other plate. Against that, it has ~5× lower routing density and is harder to keep flat over a large area: with no rigid silicon backbone, a polymer expanding at 20–50 ppm/°C bends freely and is held flat only by the dies and mold above it. What goes wrong is what goes wrong with any fan-out RDL (the Fan-Out section): cracks where a 2 µm line crosses a die edge onto a region with a different stiffness, moisture absorbed by the polyimide flashing to steam at reflow, and warpage-driven C4 opens at the corners. TSMC names no customers for it; it serves lower-I/O AI and networking ASICs with moderate HBM counts, and its real importance is as the stepping stone: the polyimide RDL, the carrier build and the release step are exactly the organic half of CoWoS-L. This module treats it as that stepping stone, in this one section, and gives the full treatment to -S and -L.

### CoWoS-L: silicon bridges in an organic interposer

**CoWoS-L** (L for local silicon interconnect) is the hybrid: an organic RDL interposer the size of the whole package, with small silicon **LSI (Local Silicon Interconnect)** bridge chiplets embedded exactly where fine-pitch routing is needed, under the edges where a GPU meets an HBM stack or where two GPU dies meet. Each LSI is a few millimetres by ten or so, fabricated on 65 nm-class tools with the same sub-micron RDL as a CoWoS-S interposer, optionally with deep-trench capacitors. Vertical connections for power, ground and slow signals go through **through-InFO vias (TIVs)**: copper pillars ~100 µm or taller, plated before the mold compound is applied and revealed by grinding. The mold compound here is the same silica-filled epoxy as in the Anatomy section, ~70–90% silica powder by weight, pressed around the parts and cured into a rigid slab (Module 16).

The interposer is built bottom-up on a **carrier**, a temporary rigid glass or silicon wafer that the structure is built on and later released from, which turns it into a **reconstituted** wafer, an artificial 300 mm disc made by placing pieces on a carrier and molding them into one body:

1. Start with a carrier wafer.
2. Build the bottom RDL layers (the future C4 side) on it.
3. Plate the TIVs as tall copper pillars through a thick mask of **photoresist** (the light-sensitive polymer that lithography patterns, Module 07): where the resist has been opened, copper grows up out of the hole.
4. Place and attach the LSI bridges at the positions where die edges will later meet.
5. Apply mold compound over bridges and pillars and cure it.
6. Grind the mold back until the TIV tops and the LSI wiring are exposed and flat.
7. Build the top RDL layers over everything, bridges and mold alike, up to the microbump pads.
8. Only then attach the GPU and HBM dies (the chip-on-wafer step of the next section).

Silicon has been reduced to the few percent of area where it earns its keep.

> **Worked example: interposer area and stitched reticles for a B200-class package.** Two ~800 mm² GPU dies (about 26 × 31 mm, long edges facing so the die-to-die link runs along ~30 mm of shared edge) plus eight HBM3E stacks of ~11 × 12 mm ≈ 130 mm²: 1,600 + 1,040 = 2,640 mm² of die. Add ~1 mm HBM-to-GPU gaps, ~1–2 mm between HBM stacks, and ~2 mm of margin for C4 fan-out and the dicing street (the gap between sites where the saw will cut); two rows of four HBM flanking the GPUs gives roughly 48 × 58 mm ≈ 2,800 mm², or 2,800 / 858 ≈ 3.3 reticles, an illustrative Blackwell-class footprint estimate. TSMC describes its first volume CoWoS-L platform as 3.5× reticle; the calculation here is a simplified floorplan, not a disclosed B200 mask layout. Since the field is 26 × 33 mm, each RDL layer of a 48 × 58 mm interposer needs a 2 × 2 array of stitched exposures (covering 52 × 66 mm with overlapping edges), so a five-layer RDL is twenty stitched fields per interposer, each stitch line held to the tolerance of the 0.4 µm lines crossing it. A 300 mm wafer (~70,700 mm²) fits ~16 such rectangles after edge exclusion, versus ~29 for H100's 2.5× interposer. The 5.5× generation (~4,700 mm², ~60 × 78 mm) needs a 3 × 3 array and fits ~9 per wafer; 9.5× (~8,000 mm², ~75 × 108 mm) fits ~4, which is the arithmetic pushing TSMC to panels.

NVIDIA's Blackwell B200 is the flagship CoWoS-L product. It needed two ~800 mm² dies with a 10 TB/s **NV-HBI** link across their shared edge (NVIDIA's proprietary die-to-die interface, described in the Chiplet section), plus eight HBM3E stacks. A 3.3× reticle CoWoS-S interposer would have been the most expensive piece of silicon in the package after the GPU dies; bridges cut that cost and removed most of the silicon-to-organic mismatch. Blackwell Ultra (B300) and Rubin are on CoWoS-L, and the 5.5× generation for 12-HBM parts was in volume production in 2026 with yields TSMC put above 98% at its 2026 Technology Symposium.

> **What can go wrong: the Blackwell delay.** CoWoS-L also nearly derailed its flagship. In mid-2024 TSMC and NVIDIA found that B200 assemblies warped during **reflow** (the oven pass that melts the solder) and **thermal cycling** (repeated swings between cold and hot to simulate a lifetime of use). As reported by SemiAnalysis and The Information, the CTE mismatch among GPU dies, LSI bridges, molded RDL interposer and substrate produced stresses that broke connections at the bridge edges. The fix required a new **mask set** (the full set of photomasks for a chip; at the 4 nm class a set costs tens of millions of dollars and a re-spin takes about a quarter) for the GPU die's top global-routing metal layers and bump layout, plus a redesign of the bridge dies, costing roughly a quarter of ramp. NVIDIA confirmed a "GPU mask" change in August 2024; TSMC has never described the failure mechanism publicly. Later NVIDIA designs were reportedly laid out with packaging stress analysis in the loop from the start.

| Variant | Interposer | Where the fine wiring lives | Min line/space | Max size (2026) | Example products | Relative cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CoWoS-S | Full silicon, TSVs | Everywhere on the interposer | ~0.4 µm | 3.3× reticle in HVM | NVIDIA A100, H100/H200; AMD MI300X and MI350 (with SoIC); Google TPU v4/v5 | High, rising steeply with area |
| CoWoS-R | Organic RDL (InFO) | Nowhere finer than ~2 µm | ~2 µm | ~3× reticle | Lower-I/O AI and networking ASICs | Low |
| CoWoS-L | Organic RDL + embedded LSI + TIVs | Only in the LSI bridges under die edges | ~0.4 µm at bridges, ~2 µm elsewhere | 3.5× in volume since 2024 (TSMC); larger-generation timing below is reported roadmap | NVIDIA B200/B300/GB200/GB300, Rubin; AMD MI400 (reported) | Medium-high |

(**HVM** is high-volume manufacturing, as opposed to pilot or qualification runs.)

## The CoWoS Process Flow, Step by Step

Here is the CoWoS-S flow from bare interposer wafer to tested package, with CoWoS-L differences noted. TSMC's recipes are proprietary; this is the publicly documented sequence and the unit processes underneath it. The overview first, then each step in depth. The time column is an order-of-magnitude guide, since TSMC publishes no cycle times.

| Step | What physically happens | Key tool | Key number | Rough time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Interposer fabrication | 10 µm holes are etched 100 µm into a 775 µm wafer and filled with copper; 4–5 damascene wiring layers are built on top in stitched exposures; the wafer is probed (tested electrically with fine needles) | Bosch etcher (Lam Syndion, TEL Tactras), plating (Lam SABRE 3D), 65 nm-class steppers | 0.4 µm lines; ~16 sites per wafer at 3.3× | ~weeks (a short wiring-only fab flow) |
| 2. Chip-on-wafer | GPU and HBM dies are placed face-down and soldered to the interposer, underfilled and over-molded | Thermocompression bonder (Besi, ASMPT) or reflow oven | 40–55 µm bump pitch; ~100,000 bumps per GPU | ~days |
| 3. Backside reveal and C4 | The molded wafer is glued to glass, ground from 775 to ~100 µm to expose the TSV tips; backside wiring and C4 bumps are formed; the glass is removed | Temporary bonder (EV Group, SUSS), grinder (Disco) | ~100 µm final thickness; 130–180 µm C4 pitch | ~days |
| 4. Singulation | The wafer is cut into chip-on-wafer modules; each is probed | Dicing saw or laser (Disco) | ~16 modules per 3.3× wafer | ~hours |
| 5. Module-on-substrate | Each module is soldered to its ABF laminate by mass reflow and underfilled | Reflow oven, flip-chip placer | ~245 °C peak; tens of thousands of C4 joints at once | ~days |
| 6. Stiffener, lid, balls, test | Ring and lid are glued on with TIM1; BGA balls attached; final test and burn-in (a hot stress test) | Lid attach, ball drop, testers (Advantest, Teradyne) | 0.6 mm balls on 1 mm pitch; 6–12 weeks end to end | ~days to weeks including burn-in |

### Step 1: Interposer fabrication

> **Intuition: why holes through the silicon, and why only 100 µm of them.** The dies sit on the interposer's top face and the substrate is under its bottom face, and the ~10,000 signals and ~1,000 A of supply current that must pass between them have only one route: straight through the slab. Hence TSVs. But a hole 10 µm across through a full 775 µm wafer would have an **aspect ratio** (depth divided by width) of 77:1, and no plasma can etch that straight, no film can coat its walls evenly, and no plating bath can fill it without sealing a void. A 100 µm-deep hole is 10:1, which can be etched, lined and filled. So the interposer is etched only 100 µm deep, everything is built on top, and the other 675 µm of silicon is ground away later (Step 3), once the wafer has the dies and mold to hold it rigid.

The interposer starts as a standard 300 mm, 775 µm prime wafer (the ordinary polished, defect-screened grade) with no **epitaxial** layer (a crystal-grown surface layer needed for transistors, not for wires), since nothing electrical is built in the silicon.
